cards.gist: Small, thin flatfish with lean, delicate, mild and sweet fillets
cards.guest: It's a small flatfish, lean and very delicate, with a mild, sweet flavor. If you like sole, it eats the same way, light and fine-flaked.
cards.why: A flatfish that lies on the seabed with both eyes on its upper side, left or right depending on the species. Little fat and thin fillets give a fine, soft texture and a mild, sweet taste. Fluke is summer flounder, and many American soles are flounders too. It cooks in minutes.
cards.note: Fluke is often served raw, sliced thin as crudo or sashimi.
cards.notThis: Not halibut, its giant cousin. Halibut comes as thick, firm portions, and flounder as thin, soft fillets or a whole fish.
cards.line: Pan-fried flounder, lemon, parsley, brown butter

cards.gist: Warm-water reef fish with lean, firm white meat in big chunky flakes
cards.guest: It's a mild white fish from the Gulf and the South Atlantic. The meat is firm and sweet with big, moist flakes, so it holds up to the grill or the fryer.
cards.why: A heavy-bodied reef fish of the sea bass family, caught off Florida, the Gulf and the Carolinas. It is lean but holds moisture well, and thick fillets break into large, firm flakes. The flavor is mild and faintly sweet, close to sea bass.
cards.notThis: Not snapper, the other Southern reef fish. Snapper fillets are thinner and finer-flaked, and grouper is chunkier and firmer.
cards.line: Blackened grouper sandwich, lettuce, tomato, tartar sauce

cards.gist: The largest flatfish, cut into thick, firm, snow-white lean portions
cards.guest: It's a big cold-water flatfish with thick, snow-white meat. Firm, clean and mildly sweet, the fish for someone who wants nothing fishy.
cards.why: The giant of the flatfish, a right-eyed flounder that can outweigh a person, from the cold North Pacific and North Atlantic. Its size gives thick portions with a firm, large flake. With very little fat, it tastes clean and mild and leans on sauce for richness.
cards.note: So lean it dries out fast. Kitchens pull it just as it turns opaque, and it is a poor choice for well done.
cards.origin: Middle English haly butte, holy flatfish, eaten on feast days
cards.notThis: Not flounder, a small flatfish sold in thin fillets, or turbot, which is richer and more gelatinous.
cards.line: Pan-roasted halibut, spring peas, beurre blanc

cards.gist: Blue-black bivalve with soft, sweet meat, steamed open in its own broth
cards.guest: They're shellfish in blue-black shells, steamed until they pop open. The meat is soft and sweet, milder than a clam, and the broth is made for dipping bread.
cards.why: A bivalve farmed in clusters on ropes, which keeps sand out. Steamed a few minutes with wine, garlic and shallot, the shells open and release their own liquor, which becomes the broth. The meat is plump and soft, sweeter and less briny than clam or oyster.
cards.note: A mussel still shut after steaming should be left in the bowl, not pried open. Orange or cream meat is only male or female.
cards.notThis: Not clams. Mussels have thin, blue-black teardrop shells and soft meat. Clams are rounder, paler and chewier.
cards.line: Steamed mussels, white wine, garlic, grilled bread

cards.gist: Rough-shelled bivalve, often eaten raw, that tastes of its home water
cards.guest: They're shellfish, and on the half shell they're shucked to order and eaten raw. A cold, silky bite of clean ocean, some brinier, some sweeter.
cards.why: A bivalve that filters the water it grows in, so each bay gives its own flavor, the way a vineyard does for wine. East Coast ones run briny and firm, West Coast ones sweeter and creamier, with a cucumber or melon note.
cards.note: On the half shell they come raw and alive on ice, opened to order. The list changes daily, so learn each name and where it grew.
cards.pairs: Mignonette, lemon, cocktail sauce, horseradish; Champagne, Chablis, Muscadet
cards.line: Half dozen oysters on the half shell, mignonette, lemon

cards.gist: Eggs of a female fish, cured loose or cooked whole in the sac
cards.guest: Roe is fish eggs. Salmon roe pops with a bright, salty burst, and spring shad roe is seared whole until it is creamy inside.
cards.why: Roe is the egg mass of a female fish, held in a thin sac. Loosened and salted, the eggs pop and taste of the sea: salmon roe is large and orange, flying fish roe tiny and crunchy. Cooked whole in the sac, like shad roe, it firms outside and turns creamy and grainy within.
cards.note: Loose salted roe, like salmon roe, is cured but never cooked: it is served raw.
cards.pairs: Blini, sour cream, chives, sushi rice, brown butter, bacon
cards.notThis: Caviar on its own means salted sturgeon roe. Any other roe sold as caviar has to name the fish, as in salmon caviar.

cards.gist: Rich, oily pink fish that grows at sea and spawns back in rivers
cards.guest: Salmon is rich and buttery, with big, silky flakes. Wild king is the richest of all, and sockeye is leaner and deeper in flavor.
cards.why: Salmon hatch in rivers, fatten at sea and swim back upstream to spawn, so they carry fat for the trip. It keeps the flesh moist and gives it big, soft flakes. The color comes from a pigment in the krill and shrimp they eat. King is the fattiest species, sockeye the reddest.
cards.note: Often served medium, still translucent in the center. Guests can ask for it cooked through.
cards.origin: Wild from Alaska to California; Atlantic salmon on menus is almost always farmed
cards.notThis: Arctic char and trout look alike but are milder, with a finer flake. Steelhead is a sea-run trout that eats much like salmon.

cards.gist: Sweet round muscle a shellfish uses to clap its two shells shut
cards.guest: Scallops are the sweet muscle that snaps the shell shut, seared golden on the outside and soft, almost creamy, in the middle.
cards.why: A scallop swims by clapping its shells, driven by one big muscle, and that muscle is what we eat. It is rich in glycogen and sweet amino acids, so it tastes sweet and browns well. Sea scallops are large and sear. Bay scallops are small and cook in seconds. Untreated dry ones sear best.
cards.note: Best seared golden and left just translucent in the center. Cooked through, they turn rubbery.
cards.notThis: Not king trumpet mushroom scallops, which are thick rounds of mushroom stem cut to look like the real thing.
cards.line: Seared sea scallops, cauliflower puree, brown butter

cards.gist: Red-skinned warm-reef fish, lean and sweet, often served whole
cards.guest: Snapper is a mild, slightly sweet white fish from warm Gulf waters. It is lean and flaky, and the skin crisps up beautifully.
cards.why: Snapper live on warm reefs in the Gulf of Mexico and the southern Atlantic. They are lean, so the flesh is mild and sweet with moist, medium flakes, and the red skin crisps well in a hot pan. Whole snapper, fried or grilled, is a classic of the Gulf and the Caribbean.
cards.note: Served whole, it arrives on the bone, with fins and small bones to work around.
cards.notThis: Not grouper, which is firmer and chunkier. West Coast Pacific snapper is usually rockfish, a different fish.
cards.line: Whole fried red snapper, green mango slaw, lime

cards.gist: Ancient armored river fish, dense and meaty, prized for its eggs
cards.guest: Sturgeon is the fish caviar comes from. The meat is firm and rich, more like veal than a flaky fish, and it is wonderful smoked.
cards.why: Sturgeon have barely changed in 200 million years: rows of bony plates, not ordinary scales, and a skeleton mostly of cartilage. The flesh has almost no flake and a good amount of fat, so it eats dense and meaty, often compared to veal or lobster, and it takes smoke beautifully.
cards.origin: Mostly farmed white sturgeon from California and Idaho; wild stocks are protected
cards.pairs: Potato pancakes, sour cream, dill, horseradish, rye bread
cards.line: Smoked sturgeon, potato pancake, sour cream, dill

cards.gist: Lean deep-water fish that eats crab, sweet and firm like lobster
cards.guest: Tilefish is a lean white fish from deep Atlantic waters. It eats crab and shrimp, so it tastes sweet, a little like lobster, with firm, moist flakes.
cards.why: Golden tilefish live at the edge of the continental shelf, digging burrows in the clay and feeding on crabs and shrimp. That diet is why the flesh tastes so sweet, often compared to lobster or scallop. It is lean, with a firm, fine flake closer to halibut than to cod.
cards.origin: Deep Atlantic shelf edge, from New England down to the Gulf of Mexico

cards.gist: Mild, delicate freshwater fish, often pan-fried whole or split
cards.guest: Trout is a mild, delicate freshwater fish with tender flakes and thin skin that crisps in the pan. With brown butter and almonds, it is a classic.
cards.why: Most trout on menus is farmed rainbow trout, raised in cold spring water in places like Idaho. It is small and fairly lean, so the flesh is mild with fine, soft flakes and the skin is thin enough to eat crisp. Steelhead is rainbow trout that went to sea: bigger, richer and pinker.
cards.note: Served whole, it keeps its fine rib bones, and butterflied fillets can still hold a few small pin bones.
cards.notThis: Arctic char is a cousin with richer, pinker flesh. Salmon is bigger and much oilier.

cards.gist: Prized European flatfish, firm and white, rich in gelatin at the bone
cards.guest: Turbot is one of the most prized fish in Europe, a flatfish with firm, snow-white flesh that is sweet and almost silky. It is often roasted whole.
cards.why: Turbot lie flat on the seabed, and their thick, muscular fillets eat firm and meaty rather than flaky. The skin and bones are rich in gelatin, which keeps the flesh moist and gives cooked turbot a silky, sticky richness that chefs pair with butter sauces.
cards.note: Often cooked on the bone to keep it juicy, so it may arrive whole or as a bone-in cut.

cards.guest: It's a deep-water fish from off the Carolinas, firm and mild with big white flakes. It eats a lot like grouper.
cards.why: It lives far down on rocky ledges off South Carolina and Georgia, and got its name from gathering around shipwrecks. Caught by hook and line in a small fishery, it is lean with large, moist, sweet flakes, much like grouper or a big sea bass.
cards.origin: Southeast US, the deep Charleston Bump; named for hanging around wrecks
cards.notThis: Not grouper, though it eats like one. It is its own deep-water family and a local Carolina catch.
cards.line: Pan-roasted wreckfish, Carolina Gold rice, brown butter

cards.gist: Salt-cured sturgeon eggs, served cold by the small spoonful
cards.guest: It's sturgeon roe, lightly salted and served cold. Each pearl pops with a clean, briny, buttery flavor, best with a blini and a glass of Champagne.
cards.why: Eggs are taken from a sturgeon, screened, and lightly salted, which firms them and seasons them without cooking. Nearly all caviar today is farmed, since wild sturgeon were overfished and wild Caspian caviar is barely traded. Osetra, Kaluga and Siberian are common kinds.

cards.guest: It's cured fish roe, dried into an amber block and grated over the dish. Salty and savory, it tastes like the sea's answer to parmesan.
cards.why: The whole roe sac of a grey mullet or a tuna is salted, pressed and air-dried for weeks until firm and amber. Drying concentrates it into a salty, savory, faintly bitter seasoning. Mullet is milder and more delicate, tuna darker and stronger.

cards.gist: Mild, lean Mediterranean white fish, often roasted and served whole
cards.guest: It's a Mediterranean sea bass, mild and delicate with crisp skin. It's often roasted whole with lemon and herbs, simple and light.
cards.why: The European sea bass, now mostly farmed in Greece and Turkey. Each fish is only a pound or two, so it suits one plate whole or as two fillets. The flesh is lean, white and finely flaked with a clean, sweet flavor, and the thin skin crisps well.
cards.note: Served whole, it comes with bones and head on. Many kitchens will fillet it before or at the table.
cards.origin: Italian name for the European sea bass; loup de mer in French
cards.notThis: Not black sea bass, the wild Atlantic fish. Branzino is the Mediterranean one, usually farmed.

cards.gist: Small wild Atlantic fish with firm, fine white flesh and crisp skin
cards.guest: It's a small wild fish from the Atlantic coast, sweet and delicate, and the skin crisps beautifully in the pan.
cards.why: A small grouper relative caught from New England to the Gulf by pot, hook and trawl. It stays small, a few pounds at most, so fillets are thin with a fine flake. The white flesh is sweet and mild, firmer than branzino, and the dark skin sears crisp.
cards.note: Thin fillets can hold a few fine pin bones.

cards.gist: Firm, buttery warm-water fish, often served raw, sturdy on a grill
cards.guest: Cobia is a firm, rich white fish from warm waters. It's buttery and clean served raw, and it holds up beautifully on the grill.
cards.why: A fast-swimming fish of warm seas, caught in the Gulf and farmed in open-ocean pens. It carries more fat than most white fish, so the meat is firm, moist and buttery with a clean, sweet flavor. Think somewhere between swordfish and snapper.
cards.note: Often served raw as crudo. Cooked, it stays moist even a little past medium.
cards.origin: Warm seas worldwide; Gulf anglers call it ling or lemonfish
cards.line: Cobia crudo, citrus, chili, olive oil

cards.gist: Big ocean hunter cut into thick, dense, mild steaks that grill well
cards.guest: Swordfish is meaty and mild, cut into thick steaks. It eats almost like a pork chop, great off the grill for someone who wants hearty fish.
cards.why: A large open-ocean fish, cut crosswise from the loin into boneless steaks. The flesh is dense with a tight grain and moderate fat, so it holds together on a grill and rarely breaks into flakes. It tastes mild, without the red-meat depth of tuna.
cards.note: The dark red band in each steak is the bloodline and is normal. Cooked past medium, it dries out fast.
cards.notThis: Not tuna, the other ocean steak. Swordfish is pale and cooked further, tuna deep red and served rare.
cards.line: Grilled swordfish, salsa verde, charred lemon

cards.gist: Deep-red, meaty ocean fish, served raw or seared rare inside
cards.guest: It's a meaty, deep-red fish, clean and rich. It's usually served raw, or seared outside and rare inside, closer to a steak than a flaky fish.
cards.why: Tuna are warm-bodied ocean sprinters, and their muscle is full of oxygen-carrying myoglobin, which makes it red and beefy. Yellowfin is lean, bigeye a little richer, and bluefin belly is marbled with fat. Albacore is the paler, milder one canned as white tuna.
cards.note: Usually served raw or rare. Cooked through, it firms up, dries and tastes like canned tuna.
cards.pairs: Soy, sesame, ginger, avocado, wasabi, citrus

cards.guest: It's a firm, sweet white fish people call poor man's lobster. It holds together like a steak instead of flaking.
cards.why: Monkfish is an anglerfish, mostly head and mouth, so the tail is the main cut sold. That tail is dense, springy muscle around one central bone, with no flakes, so it eats sweet and meaty like shellfish and stands up to roasting, grilling and stews.

cards.guest: Sweet, firm shrimp, cooked just until they curl and turn pink, so they stay juicy with a little snap.

cards.gist: Chesapeake swimmer prized for sweet, hand-picked lump meat
cards.guest: It's the East Coast crab Maryland crab cakes are famous for. The meat is sweet and delicate, and the big jumbo lumps are the prize.
cards.why: A swimming crab of the Atlantic and Gulf with paddle-shaped back legs. The two big muscles driving those paddles give jumbo lump, the whitest, sweetest meat. Lump and backfin are smaller pieces, and claw meat is darker and stronger. Picking is slow handwork, hence the price.
cards.note: Hand-picked meat can hold small bits of shell and cartilage, even when picked carefully.
cards.origin: Atlantic and Gulf coasts, most famously Maryland's Chesapeake Bay
cards.pairs: Old Bay, drawn butter, crab cakes, remoulade, cold beer
cards.line: Jumbo lump blue crab cake, remoulade, charred lemon

cards.gist: Freshly molted Chesapeake swimmer, eaten whole with its legs
cards.guest: It's a blue crab caught just after it sheds its old shell, so you eat the whole thing. Crisp outside, sweet and juicy inside.
cards.why: Crabs grow by molting: they split the old shell and back out soft. Within hours the new one starts to firm, so watermen hold molting crabs in tanks and pull them the moment they emerge. The kitchen trims the face, gills and apron, then fries or sautés it whole.
cards.note: Eaten entirely, legs and all. The light crunch of the new shell is the point, not a mistake.
cards.origin: A late spring to summer delicacy, mostly from the Chesapeake Bay
cards.line: Fried soft-shell crab, remoulade, pickled green tomato

cards.gist: Big-clawed cold-water crustacean with a firm, sweet tail
cards.guest: It's the cold-water Atlantic kind with big claws. The tail is firm and sweet, the claw meat softer, and it all loves butter.
cards.why: A North Atlantic crustacean fished mostly off Maine and Canada. The tail is one big muscle, so it eats firm and snappy, while claws and knuckles are sweeter and softer. The meat breaks down fast after death, so it is cooked live or killed just before.
cards.note: The green paste in the body is tomalley, and dark beads in a female are roe, called coral, which turn red when cooked.
cards.notThis: Not spiny or rock lobster, a warm-water cousin with no big claws, usually sold as tails.
cards.line: Butter-poached Maine lobster, sweet corn, tarragon

cards.gist: Sand-burrowing two-shelled shellfish, briny and chewy
cards.guest: Clams are briny little shellfish with a pleasant chew. Small ones like littlenecks are eaten raw or steamed open in wine and garlic.
cards.why: Two-shelled animals that burrow in sand and mud and filter the water, so they taste of where they grew. Hard shells sell by size: littlenecks small and tender, cherrystones bigger, chowder clams biggest, tough and chopped. Soft-shell steamers have a neck skin to peel.
cards.note: Sold alive with shells shut. Littlenecks and cherrystones are often served raw on the half shell.
cards.notThis: Not mussels, which are longer, blue-black and smooth, and cling to rocks and ropes instead of burrowing.
cards.line: Linguine with littleneck clams, white wine, chili

cards.gist: Thick, gray-brown cap from the oyster mushroom family, springy
cards.guest: It's a thick, meaty cousin of the oyster mushroom, named for the shellfish because it has the same firm, springy chew. Seared, it's savory and satisfying.
cards.why: A close relative of the oyster mushroom, grown indoors on sawdust or straw, mostly in East Asia. Its caps are thicker and denser than an oyster's, so they keep their shape and a firm, springy chew when seared or braised. The name comes from that chew.
cards.origin: Named for abalone, the prized sea snail its chewy texture resembles
cards.notThis: Not abalone, the shellfish. A mushroom named for its chew, though it is often braised in oyster sauce.
cards.line: Seared abalone mushroom, black garlic, scallion

cards.gist: Clump of round brown or white caps, bitter raw and nutty cooked
cards.guest: They're little clustered mushrooms, brown or white, on long stems. Cooked, they turn nutty and a bit sweet, with a pleasant crunch that holds up.
cards.why: Grown in bottles of sawdust, they reach the kitchen as a clump joined at the base, which is trimmed to free them. Raw they taste bitter, but cooking turns them nutty and savory, and unlike softer mushrooms they stay firm and slightly crunchy.
cards.origin: Japanese buna-shimeji, named for the beech logs it grows on in the wild
cards.pairs: Butter, soy, miso, ramen, rice dishes and hot pots
cards.line: Roasted beech mushrooms, miso butter, scallion

cards.gist: Thin, hollow, near-black wild funnel with a deep, smoky flavor
cards.guest: It's a wild mushroom shaped like a little dark horn. It's thin and delicate, with a deep, smoky flavor, a bit like truffle, that goes a long way.
cards.why: A wild relative of the chanterelle, foraged under hardwoods and not farmed. It has no gills, just a thin hollow funnel, so it cooks in a minute and turns silky. Its aroma is intense and smoky, and it dries so well that dried ones are ground into sauces.
cards.note: The hollow funnel traps forest grit, so kitchens split and rinse each one.
cards.origin: French trompette de la mort, for its dark color and All Saints' season
cards.notThis: Not king trumpet, the thick white farmed stem. This one is wild, thin and nearly black.
cards.line: Black trumpet risotto, parmesan, brown butter

cards.gist: Golden, vase-shaped wild mushroom, apricot-scented and peppery
cards.guest: It's a golden wild mushroom, foraged, not farmed. It smells faintly of apricot and has a gentle, peppery flavor and a tender, meaty bite.
cards.why: Chanterelles live in partnership with the roots of living trees, which is why they are not grown commercially and nearly all are foraged. Under the cap they carry blunt ridges, not true gills. Firm and a little chewy, they taste fruity and peppery, milder than porcini.
cards.origin: French, from Greek kantharos, a drinking cup, for its shape
cards.pairs: Brown butter, sweet corn, eggs, roast chicken, white Burgundy
cards.line: Pan-roasted chanterelles, sweet corn, brown butter

cards.gist: Ruffled cluster of gray-brown fronds found at the base of oak trees
cards.guest: It's maitake, a big, ruffled mushroom that grows wild under oaks and is farmed too. Roasted, the frilly edges crisp up and the center stays tender and earthy.
cards.why: It grows as one large rosette of overlapping gray-brown caps, usually at the base of oaks, and is now widely farmed too. Torn into pieces and roasted or seared, the thin edges crisp like chips while the thick base stays meaty. The flavor is deep and earthy.
cards.origin: The Japanese name, maitake, means dancing mushroom
cards.notThis: Not chicken of the woods, a bright orange shelf fungus. This one is gray-brown and ruffled.
cards.line: Crispy maitake, miso butter, charred scallion

cards.gist: Thick white stem under a small cap, seared in coins like scallops
cards.guest: It's a mushroom that's almost all thick white stem. Seared, it's firm and meaty with a mild, savory flavor, and some cooks cut it into coins like scallops.
cards.why: The largest of the oyster mushroom family, farmed on sawdust. Unlike most mushrooms, its stem is the prize: dense and firm, it browns deeply, shrinks less than softer kinds and keeps a springy bite. Cooks score it and sear it like a scallop or a steak.
cards.origin: Native to Mediterranean grasslands, now farmed worldwide as eryngii
cards.notThis: Not black trumpet, the thin dark wild funnel. This one is thick, white and farmed.
cards.line: Seared king oyster mushroom, brown butter, capers

cards.gist: Hollow, honeycombed spring mushroom, always cooked through
cards.guest: It's a wild spring mushroom with a honeycombed cap, one of the most prized there is. It's nutty and earthy, and all those pockets soak up the sauce.
cards.why: Morels come up for a few weeks each spring in woods, old orchards and burned forest, and most are still foraged, hence the price. The cap is a hollow honeycomb, light and chewy, and its pits hold butter or cream. The flavor is deep, nutty and meaty, stronger still when dried.
cards.note: Always cooked through: raw or undercooked morels can make people sick. The pits also trap grit.
cards.pairs: Asparagus, spring peas, ramps, cream sauces, veal and chicken
cards.line: Morels and asparagus, cream, grilled bread

cards.gist: Soft, fan-shaped gray caps growing in shelves, mild and velvety
cards.guest: They're soft, fan-shaped mushrooms with a mild, gently savory flavor. Seared hot, the thin edges go crisp and golden while the middle stays velvety.
cards.why: Grown on straw or sawdust, they form overlapping shelves of thin, tender caps with short stems. Being thin, they cook in minutes, and a hot pan crisps the edges. The name is for the shell-like shape and color, not the taste, which is mild with a faint sweetness.
cards.note: Golden and pink kinds sold under the same name are thinner and cook even faster.
cards.notThis: Not oysters, the shellfish. The name is for the cap's shape, though dishes may use oyster sauce.
cards.line: Crispy oyster mushrooms, chili crisp, scallion

cards.gist: Brown East Asian mushroom with a smoky, deeply savory bite
cards.guest: It's a mushroom from East Asia grown on hardwood, meaty and smoky with a deep savory flavor. It's wonderful off the grill or in a broth.
cards.why: It grows on hardwood logs or sawdust blocks. Cutting and cooking release a sulfur aroma compound, and the cap is rich in the compounds behind umami, stronger still once dried. The cap eats meaty and firm; the stem is woody, so kitchens keep it for stock.
cards.note: Meant to be cooked through: raw or undercooked shiitake gives a few people an itchy, streaky rash.
cards.origin: Japanese, from shii, the tree it grows on, and take, mushroom
cards.pairs: Soy, ginger, miso, kombu broth, noodles, rice
cards.line: Grilled shiitake, miso butter, scallion, rice

cards.gist: Rare underground fungus found by dogs, prized for its aroma
cards.guest: It's a rare fungus that grows underground on tree roots, and dogs sniff it out. It's usually shaved fresh over the dish, and the smell is the whole point.
cards.why: A truffle fruits underground on the roots of oak and hazel, and it spreads by smell, so it is hunted with trained dogs. Its value is aroma, which fades within days of digging, so it is bought small and used fast: white shaved raw, black often warmed gently in fat.
cards.origin: Black winter truffles from France, white from Piedmont in Italy
cards.notThis: Not the chocolate truffle, which is a candy, and not truffle oil, which is usually just flavored.
cards.line: Tagliatelle, butter, shaved black truffle

cards.gist: Finishing drizzle whose truffle scent usually comes from a lab
cards.guest: It's an oil flavored to smell like truffle, drizzled on at the end. It gives a big, earthy hit of that aroma.
cards.why: Most bottles are olive or neutral oil flavored with a manufactured copy of one aroma compound found in white truffle, sometimes with a speck of real truffle for show. It smells louder and flatter than the real thing, and heat drives the aroma off, so it goes on at the end.
cards.note: A few drops go a long way. Too much reads harsh and chemical.
cards.notThis: Not the truffle itself. If a guest asks for real truffle, the answer is the shaved fresh truffle, not the oil.
cards.line: Fries, truffle oil, parmesan, parsley

cards.gist: Fat-stemmed wild forest mushroom with a sponge under its cap
cards.guest: Porcini are wild forest mushrooms with a deep, nutty, almost meaty flavor. They're a classic in risotto and fresh pasta.
cards.why: A wild mushroom that lives with the roots of pine, oak and spruce and resists farming, so it is foraged. Under the cap is a sponge of pores, not gills. Drying concentrates its nutty, beefy flavor, which is why most kitchens use dried, and the soaking water becomes stock.
cards.origin: Italian for little pigs; the French call it cèpe
cards.pairs: Risotto, fresh pasta, veal, beef, polenta, parmesan
cards.line: Porcini risotto, parmesan, brown butter

cards.gist: Brown strain of the everyday button, firmer and a little earthier
cards.guest: It's the brown cousin of the white button mushroom, a little firmer with more flavor. Let it grow bigger and you get a portobello.
cards.why: Same species as the white button: the button is a pale mutant found in a brown bed in the 1920s, and cremini is the original brown strain. It has a touch less water and a deeper, earthier flavor, so it browns well and holds shape. Grown to full size, it is sold as a portobello.
cards.notThis: Not a wild mushroom. It is farmed year round, the everyday brown mushroom.
cards.line: Roasted cremini, garlic, thyme, sherry

cards.gist: Bundle of long, thin white stems with pinhead caps and a crunch
cards.guest: Enoki are long, thin white mushrooms that grow in a bundle. They're mild and a little crunchy, and they soak up the broth they cook in.
cards.why: Farmed in dark bottles with little air, it stretches into pale noodle-like stems instead of the short golden caps it grows in the wild. There is little cap, so it eats crisp and springy rather than meaty, with a mild, faintly fruity flavor that takes on broth.
cards.note: Cook it through. Packaged enoki has been part of US listeria recalls, so it should not go out raw.
cards.origin: Japanese, from enoki, the hackberry tree it grows on wild
cards.line: Beef hot pot, enoki, napa cabbage, tofu

cards.gist: Shaggy white ball of spines that sears up like crab meat
cards.guest: It's a white, shaggy mushroom that sears up tender and flaky, a lot like crab or lobster. The flavor is mild and a little sweet.
cards.why: It grows on hardwood trees as a white mop of hanging spines, with no gills or cap. Those spines are fine and fibrous, so pressed and seared hard it pulls into strands like shellfish meat. It holds a lot of water, so it needs a hot pan to brown instead of steaming.
cards.pairs: Brown butter, lemon, capers, crab cake style with remoulade
cards.line: Seared lion's mane, brown butter, capers

cards.gist: Orange shelf fungus off tree trunks that tears into meaty strands
cards.guest: It's a wild orange mushroom that grows in shelves on trees. Cooked, it pulls apart like chicken breast, with a mild, slightly lemony flavor.
cards.why: A wild shelf fungus foraged from the trunks of living and dead hardwoods, oak above all, in summer and fall. Its flesh is dense and fibrous rather than soft, so it tears into strands like cooked chicken. Only the young, tender edges eat well; the older core turns woody.
cards.note: Must be cooked through. A few people get an upset stomach even from cooked pieces.
cards.notThis: Not hen of the woods, the gray frilly maitake. This one is bright orange-yellow shelves.
cards.line: Fried chicken of the woods, hot honey, pickles

cards.gist: Cheese made from ewe's milk, rich and sweet, sold fresh or aged
cards.guest: It's a sheep's milk cheese, richer and sweeter than most cow's milk cheeses, with a nutty, buttery finish.
cards.why: Sheep's milk carries nearly twice the fat and more protein than cow's milk, so the cheese eats dense, creamy and sweet. Young, it is mild and milky. Aged, as in the Pyrenees tommes like Ossau-Iraty, it turns firm, nutty and caramel-like.
cards.origin: French for ewe, used for sheep's milk cheeses, above all from the Pyrenees
cards.pairs: Black cherry jam, quince paste, walnuts, crusty bread
cards.line: Aged brebis, black cherry jam, walnut bread

cards.gist: Thick, tangy cultured milk that tenderizes batters and brines
cards.guest: It's a tangy, lightly thick cultured milk, the classic secret to tender biscuits and juicy fried chicken.
cards.why: Once the liquid left after churning butter, today it is low-fat milk soured with lactic cultures. Its acid loosens meat proteins in a brine and reacts with baking soda in batters for lift. It tastes like thin, sharp yogurt, not butter.
cards.pairs: Fried chicken, biscuits, pancakes, ranch dressing
cards.line: Buttermilk fried chicken, hot honey, slaw

cards.gist: Soft, bright, tangy fresh cheese made from goat's milk
cards.guest: It's fresh goat cheese, creamy and bright with a clean tang. It's lovely with beets, honey or a warm salad.
cards.why: Goat's milk is set slowly with cultures and a little rennet, then drained into soft logs. The cultures give the lemony tang, goat's milk fatty acids the goaty note. Young it is spreadable, like tangier cream cheese. Aged, it firms and grows a rind.
cards.origin: French for goat, used in America for fresh goat cheese
cards.pairs: Roasted beets, honey, figs, arugula, toasted walnuts
cards.notThis: Not feta, which is brined, saltier and firmer. Chèvre is soft, creamy and never sits in brine.
cards.line: Roasted beets, whipped chèvre, pistachio, honey

cards.gist: Thick, mild cultured cream that won't curdle when hot
cards.guest: It's French cultured cream, thick and rich with a gentle tang, like a silkier, milder sour cream. It melts into anything warm.
cards.why: Heavy cream is ripened with lactic cultures until it thickens and turns softly sour. With about twice the fat of sour cream, it can go into a hot pan sauce without splitting, and it tastes nutty and mellow rather than sharp.
cards.origin: French, fresh cream, though it is cultured, not plain
cards.pairs: Caviar, smoked salmon, potatoes, fruit tarts
cards.notThis: Not sour cream, which is leaner and sharper and curdles in a hot sauce.
cards.line: Smoked trout, potato rosti, crème fraîche, dill

cards.gist: Smooth, spoonable soft white cheese, mild and lightly sour
cards.guest: It's a fresh French cheese, smooth and spoonable like thick yogurt, cool and mildly tangy.
cards.why: Milk, often skimmed, is soured with cultures and a touch of rennet, then drained only briefly, so the curd stays wet and silky. It is never aged. Think smoother than ricotta and milder than Greek yogurt, with fat set by the milk used.
cards.origin: French for white cheese, a staple of French breakfasts and desserts
cards.pairs: Berries and honey, or herbs, shallot and black pepper
cards.notThis: Not ricotta, which is grainier and made by heating. This is smooth, tangy and set without heat.
cards.line: Fromage blanc, strawberries, honey, cracked pepper

cards.gist: Hard, long-aged Italian cow's milk cheese, nutty and salty
cards.guest: It's a hard, long-aged cheese, nutty and savory with little crunchy crystals. It makes everything taste deeper.
cards.why: The real one is made around Parma from raw, part-skimmed cow's milk and aged 12 months or far longer. As it ages, proteins break down into savory amino acids, which is where the depth comes from. The crunchy white specks are clusters of one of them, tyrosine.
cards.origin: English for Parmigiano-Reggiano, though US parmesan can be domestic
cards.pairs: Pasta, risotto, balsamic, pears, Caesar salad
cards.line: Shaved Parmigiano-Reggiano, arugula, lemon

cards.gist: Mild, pale butterfat, most milk solids skimmed off before they brown
cards.guest: It's butter melted down to its golden fat, with the milky bits skimmed off. It tastes clean and buttery and can take real heat.
cards.why: Butter is gently melted so the water cooks off and the milk solids separate. The solids burn first in a hot pan, so with most of them gone the fat can sear without scorching. It keeps a mild butter flavor and is the classic base for hollandaise.
cards.pairs: Lobster, crab, hollandaise, béarnaise, seared fish
cards.notThis: Not ghee, which is cooked longer until the solids toast. That tastes nutty. This stays clean and mild.
cards.line: Steamed lobster, drawn butter, lemon

cards.gist: Butter cooked until its milk solids toast, left in for a nutty taste
cards.guest: It's butter cooked just until it toasts, so it turns golden and smells like hazelnuts. It's rich and warm.
cards.why: As butter cooks, its water boils off and the milk solids fall to the bottom and toast, the same browning that colors bread crust. That gives a nutty, caramel flavor plain melted butter lacks. The French call it hazelnut butter for the color and smell.
cards.note: It goes from toasted to burnt in seconds, so it is usually made to order.
cards.pairs: Sage and squash pasta, sole, scallops, cakes
cards.notThis: Not ghee, which toasts the solids and then strains them out. Brown butter keeps them in, and that is the flavor.
cards.line: Butternut squash agnolotti, brown butter, sage

cards.gist: Butter simmered until its milk solids toast, then strained out
cards.guest: It's butter cooked slowly until golden and nutty, then strained, for a rich, toasty butter flavor you can't get from plain butter.
cards.why: Butter is simmered until its water cooks off and the milk solids sink and toast, then it is strained. What remains is nearly pure butterfat with a nutty, caramel flavor that keeps at room temperature and takes high heat without burning.
cards.origin: India and South Asia, where it is the everyday cooking fat
cards.notThis: Clarified butter is strained before the solids color. Brown butter keeps its toasted solids in. Ghee toasts them, then strains them out.
cards.line: Ghee-roasted cauliflower, cumin, yogurt, mint

cards.gist: Butter beaten with herbs, chilled in a log, sliced onto hot food
cards.guest: It's butter mixed with herbs and seasonings, then chilled. A slice melts over your steak and turns into the sauce.
cards.why: Softened butter is beaten with herbs, garlic, shallot, citrus or spices, rolled into a log and chilled. A cold slice set on hot steak or fish melts into an instant sauce that carries those flavors. The French classic is maître d'hôtel butter, parsley and lemon.
cards.pairs: Grilled steak, fish, corn on the cob, warm bread
cards.line: Seared strip steak, herb compound butter, fries

cards.gist: Silky Italian cheese of cream set with a mild acid, not rennet
cards.guest: It's an Italian cream cheese, silky, sweet and very rich. It's what makes tiramisu so plush, like cream cheese with barely any tang.
cards.why: Cream, not milk, is warmed and set with a food acid such as citric acid, then drained. With no rennet and no aging it stays spoonable, sweet and only faintly tangy, and because it starts as cream it is far richer than cream cheese.
cards.origin: Lombardy, in northern Italy
cards.pairs: Tiramisu, fresh figs, berries and honey, risotto
cards.notThis: Not ricotta, which is fluffy, grainy curds from whey. Mascarpone is smooth, dense and made from cream.
cards.line: Tiramisu, espresso-soaked ladyfingers, mascarpone, cocoa

cards.gist: Soft, fluffy curds made by reheating the whey left from cheesemaking
cards.guest: It's a soft, fluffy fresh cheese with a sweet, milky flavor. Whipped with honey, it's like a cloud on toast.
cards.why: The name means recooked: whey left from making other cheeses is heated again, often with milk and a little acid, until the last proteins float up as soft curds. Drained, they are light, moist and mildly sweet. Ricotta salata is the pressed, salted, firm version.
cards.origin: Italy, a by-product of cheesemaking
cards.pairs: Honey, lemon zest, ravioli, lasagna, grilled bread
cards.notThis: Not mascarpone, which is dense set cream, or fromage blanc, which is smooth and tangy. Ricotta is light, fluffy curds.
cards.line: Whipped ricotta, hot honey, grilled bread

cards.gist: Pouch of stretched cheese curd filled with cream-soaked shreds
cards.guest: It's a ball of fresh mozzarella filled with cream and soft curd. Cut it open and the center spills out, rich and milky.
cards.why: Mozzarella curd is stretched in hot water into a thin pouch, filled with stracciatella, shreds of the same curd soaked in cream, then tied shut. The shell is springy and the center loose and sweet, so it eats richer than plain mozzarella.
cards.note: Best within a day or two of making, and served at room temperature, not fridge-cold.
cards.origin: Puglia, southern Italy; the name comes from the Italian for butter
cards.notThis: Not fresh mozzarella, which is solid all the way through. Burrata has a creamy, spoonable center.
cards.line: Burrata, heirloom tomatoes, basil oil, grilled bread

cards.gist: Soft white ball of stretched milk curd, solid through, kept in liquid
cards.guest: It's soft, milky mozzarella made fresh and kept in water, nothing like the shredded kind. Sweet, delicate and a little springy.
cards.why: Curds are dipped in hot water and pulled like taffy until smooth and elastic, then shaped into balls and kept in water or whey. Unaged, it tastes of sweet milk with a light tang and melts into soft strings. Low-moisture pizza mozzarella is the drier cousin.
cards.origin: Southern Italy; from mozzare, to cut off, as the curd is pinched off by hand
cards.notThis: Not burrata, which is a mozzarella pouch filled with cream. This is the same curd, solid all the way through.
cards.line: Fresh mozzarella, tomato, basil, olive oil

cards.gist: Salty, tangy white cheese of sheep and goat milk, aged in brine
cards.guest: It's the Greek brined cheese, crumbly and creamy with a salty, tangy bite. It wakes up salads, watermelon and anything off the grill.
cards.why: Curds are cut into slabs, salted and aged in brine for at least two months. The brine keeps it moist and sharply salty, and sheep's milk gives a rich, creamy tang. In the EU only Greek cheese of sheep's milk, with up to 30 percent goat, carries the name.
cards.origin: Greece; the name means slice, for the slabs it is cut into
cards.pairs: Greek salad, watermelon, olives, spanakopita, honey
cards.notThis: Not chèvre, which is soft, unbrined goat cheese. Feta is firmer, saltier and aged in brine.
cards.line: Baked feta, cherry tomatoes, oregano, warm pita

cards.gist: Wheel pierced so a mold culture grows in veins, sharp, salty, creamy
cards.guest: It's cheese ripened with a mold that runs through it in blue veins. Sharp, salty and creamy, it's bold, and wonderful with pears or honey.
cards.why: Milk is set with a blue mold culture, then the young wheel is pierced with needles. Air rushing in lets the mold grow blue-green veins that break down fat and protein, giving the peppery bite and creamy texture. Gorgonzola, Roquefort and Stilton are all in this family.
cards.note: Serve it at room temperature and taste it last on a board, since it overpowers milder cheeses.
cards.pairs: Pears, walnuts, honey, port, steak, wedge salad
cards.line: Iceberg wedge, blue cheese, bacon, cherry tomato

cards.gist: Soft cheese under a velvety white mold skin that ripens it inward
cards.guest: It's a soft cheese with a thin, velvety white rind, like Brie or Camembert. Inside it's buttery and creamy, with a mild mushroomy flavor.
cards.why: The young cheese is dusted or sprayed with white molds, which grow a downy skin within about a week. Those molds soften the curd from the outside in, so a ripe one runs creamy under the rind and tastes of butter, cream and mushroom. The rind is edible.
cards.note: Best served at room temperature. A firm, chalky center means it is young, and that is normal.
cards.pairs: Baguette, honey, fig jam, apples, Champagne
cards.notThis: Not a washed rind. A bloomy rind is white, velvety and mild, while a washed rind is orange, sticky and pungent.
cards.line: Bloomy rind cheese, honeycomb, grilled baguette

cards.gist: Brine-bathed aging cheese with a sticky orange skin and strong aroma
cards.guest: It's a cheese like Taleggio, rubbed with brine as it ages, so the rind turns orange and smells bold. Inside it's milder, soft and savory.
cards.why: While it ages the cheese is rubbed with brine, sometimes with beer, wine or brandy. The damp, salty surface grows orange bacteria that make the tacky rind and barnyard smell, while the paste stays supple and savory. Think Taleggio or French Munster.
cards.note: The rind is edible but strong, and many guests leave it.
cards.pairs: Belgian ale, Alsatian white wine, pear, rye bread
cards.notThis: Not a bloomy rind. A washed rind is orange, tacky and pungent, while a bloomy rind is white, velvety and mild.
cards.line: Washed rind cheese, pear mostarda, rye crisps

cards.gist: Pinched pockets of Piedmontese egg pasta, stuffed with roast meat
cards.guest: They're little pinched pillows of fresh egg pasta from Piedmont, classically filled with roast meat. Small, tender, and made to soak up the sauce.
cards.why: A long strip of egg dough is folded over a line of filling, then pinched and cut into bite-size pockets, so each one has a ruffled edge that grabs sauce. The classic filling is leftover braised or roast meat, so they eat richer than cheese ravioli.
cards.origin: Piedmont, northern Italy; pinched ones are agnolotti del plin, plin meaning pinch
cards.notThis: Not ravioli, which are larger squares sealed between two sheets, and not tortellini, which are rings wrapped around a finger.
cards.line: Veal agnolotti, brown butter, sage, parmesan

cards.gist: Dark, earthy seed of a plant related to rhubarb, not a true grain
cards.guest: It's the dark, earthy seed of a plant related to rhubarb, ground into flour for crepes and noodles. It tastes toasty, a bit like dark rye.
cards.why: The three-sided seeds are hulled into groats, eaten whole or ground into flour. Toasted groats, called kasha, taste deep and nutty. The flour is gray and earthy, the backbone of Japanese soba, Breton galettes and Russian blini.
cards.note: Soba, blini and many buckwheat crepes are blended with wheat flour, so ask the kitchen what is in each one.
cards.origin: From Dutch boekweit, beech wheat, for seeds shaped like beechnuts
cards.line: Buckwheat crepe, ham, gruyere, fried egg

cards.gist: Wheat parboiled, dried and cracked, so it softens in minutes
cards.guest: It's cracked wheat that's already been cooked once, so it's light and fluffy with a nutty chew. It's the grain in tabbouleh.
cards.why: Whole wheat kernels are boiled, dried and cracked into fine, medium or coarse bits. Because the starch is cooked before it is cracked, it only needs soaking or a short simmer, and the grains stay separate and chewy rather than going mushy.
cards.origin: Turkey and the Levant; the grain behind tabbouleh, kibbeh and pilaf
cards.notThis: Not couscous, which is tiny rolled pasta made from semolina. Bulgur is broken grain and eats nuttier and chewier.
cards.line: Tabbouleh, bulgur, parsley, mint, lemon

cards.gist: Ancient hulled wheat, usually emmer, with a big chewy, nutty grain
cards.guest: It's an ancient Italian wheat with a big, chewy grain and a nutty flavor. It holds its bite, so it's great in salads and risotto-style dishes.
cards.why: It is hulled wheat, mostly emmer, whose husk clings to the grain. Pearled farro has the bran rubbed off and cooks in about 20 minutes. Whole farro keeps it and takes longer, staying firmer and nuttier. Think brown rice with more bounce.
cards.pairs: Mushrooms, roasted squash, pecorino, grain salads
cards.notThis: Not barley, though it looks similar. On Italian labels piccolo means einkorn, medio emmer and grande spelt.
cards.line: Farro salad, roasted squash, pecorino, brown butter
cards.prompt: It is hulled wheat, mostly emmer, whose husk clings to the grain. Pearled __ has the bran rubbed off and cooks in about 20 minutes. Whole __ keeps it and takes longer, staying firmer and nuttier. Think brown rice with more bounce.

cards.gist: Tiny, tender grain of one of the very first wheats ever farmed
cards.guest: It's einkorn, one of the oldest wheats people farmed. The grains are tiny and tender, with a mild, sweet, nutty flavor.
cards.why: Piccolo is einkorn, one of the first wheats people farmed, about ten thousand years ago. Its kernels are small, so it cooks faster and eats softer and sweeter than everyday farro, which is emmer. It is a true wheat, just an old one.
cards.origin: Italian for small farro; einkorn, first farmed in what is now Turkey
cards.notThis: Not plain farro, which is usually emmer with a bigger, chewier grain. Piccolo on the label is what marks it.
cards.line: Einkorn risotto, spring peas, lemon, parmesan
