cards.gist: Soft little dumplings of riced potato bound with a bit of flour
cards.guest: They're soft little potato dumplings, light and pillowy. Think of the best mashed potato shaped into bite-size pieces.
cards.why: Baked or boiled potato is riced, then kneaded with just enough flour to hold. Less flour and a light hand keep them tender. Too much work makes them dense. They boil in about two minutes, and many kitchens then sear them for a crisp edge.
cards.pairs: Brown butter and sage, tomato sauce, gorgonzola cream, pesto
cards.notThis: Not rolled pasta, though flour binds them. Ricotta gnocchi swap potato for cheese, and gnocchi alla romana are baked semolina discs.
cards.line: Potato gnocchi, brown butter, sage, parmesan

cards.gist: Coarsely ground dried corn, slow-cooked into a Southern porridge
cards.guest: Grits are ground dried corn slow-cooked until creamy, often finished with butter. It's the South's comfort food, and great under shrimp.
cards.why: Dried corn, often dent corn or lime-treated hominy, is ground coarse and simmered in water or milk until the starch swells. Stone-ground grits keep the germ, so they taste more of corn and take up to an hour. Instant grits cook in minutes and taste flat.
cards.pairs: Shrimp, grillades, fried eggs, country ham, red-eye gravy
cards.notThis: Not polenta, the Italian cousin. Grits are Southern, often from white corn, and usually cooked looser and butterier.
cards.line: Shrimp and grits, tasso gravy, scallions
cards.prompt: Dried corn, often dent corn or lime-treated hominy, is ground coarse and simmered in water or milk until the starch swells. Stone-ground __ keep the germ, so they taste more of corn and take up to an hour. Instant __ cook in minutes and taste flat.

cards.gist: Italian cornmeal cooked into a porridge, served soft or set and grilled
cards.guest: It's Italian cornmeal slow-cooked until creamy, often with butter and cheese. Served soft it's like a savory corn pudding, and set and grilled it gets a crisp crust.
cards.why: Dried corn is ground to meal and stirred into simmering liquid until the starch swells. Served soft, it is spoonable and creamy. Left to cool, it sets firm and can be sliced, then grilled or fried. Coarse meal tastes more of corn and takes longer.
cards.origin: Northern Italy; Latin polenta meant barley meal, long before corn arrived
cards.pairs: Braised meats, mushrooms, ragu, gorgonzola
cards.notThis: Not grits, the Southern cousin. Polenta is usually yellow corn and is served soft or set firm.
cards.line: Braised short rib, soft polenta, gremolata

cards.gist: Tiny Andean seed that cooks up fluffy with a little curled tail
cards.guest: It's a tiny seed from the Andes, cooked like rice. It's light and fluffy with a gentle pop and a nutty, earthy flavor.
cards.why: Not a grass grain at all but the seed of a plant related to spinach and beets. Simmered, each seed turns translucent and its germ loosens into a white spiral, which gives the soft pop. It is lighter than rice or farro and carries dressings well.
cards.note: The seed's natural coating is bitter and soapy, so it is rinsed before cooking. Most sold today comes prewashed.
cards.origin: Andes of Bolivia and Peru, grown there for thousands of years
cards.notThis: Not couscous, which is tiny pasta rolled from wheat. Quinoa is a seed, and each one shows a little curled tail.
cards.line: Red quinoa, roasted squash, pepitas, lemon

cards.gist: Italian rice stirred with hot broth until creamy from its own starch
cards.guest: It's Italian rice stirred slowly in broth until it turns creamy on its own, then finished with butter and parmesan. Rich, with a little bite.
cards.why: Short, starchy rice is toasted in fat, then fed hot broth a ladle at a time. The stirring rubs starch off each grain into the liquid, making a sauce with no cream, while the core stays firm. Butter and cheese beaten in at the end make it glossy.
cards.note: It keeps thickening as it sits, so run it to the table the moment it is up.
cards.origin: Northern Italy, from riso, the Italian word for rice
cards.pairs: Saffron, mushrooms, seafood, spring peas, osso buco
cards.line: Wild mushroom risotto, aged parmesan, thyme

cards.gist: Long, firm Italian risotto rice variety bred near Milan in 1945
cards.guest: It's the rice many Italian chefs choose for risotto. It turns just as creamy but each grain stays distinct with a pleasant bite.
cards.why: An Italian superfino rice bred near Milan in the 1940s. Its outside sheds plenty of starch for creaminess, but the grain is longer and firmer than arborio and holds its shape, so the risotto is more forgiving and less likely to turn mushy.
cards.origin: Bred in Lombardy in 1945, grown in Piedmont and Lombardy
cards.notThis: Not arborio, the plumper, softer risotto rice. Carnaroli grains are longer and stay firmer in the pan.
cards.line: Carnaroli risotto, saffron, bone marrow

cards.gist: Husk-aged risotto rice brand, its germ put back once milled
cards.guest: It's a prized Italian risotto rice, aged at least a year before milling, so the grains stay firm and soak up the broth.
cards.why: A carnaroli rice from one family estate near Vercelli in Piedmont. It is aged in the husk at least a year, which firms the starch so grains absorb broth without splitting. After milling, the germ is blended back in, adding nutrients and a little nuttiness.
cards.origin: Tenuta Colombara estate in Piedmont, Italian for watercolor
cards.notThis: Not a variety but a brand: aged carnaroli from a single Piedmont estate, sold in tins.
cards.line: Aged Acquerello risotto, white truffle, parmesan

cards.gist: Coarse, sandy golden meal milled from hard durum wheat
cards.guest: It's coarse, golden flour milled from hard durum wheat, what most dried pasta is made from. It gives pasta and bread a firm bite and a warm yellow color.
cards.why: Durum wheat is so hard that milling shatters it into sandy, yellow grit instead of soft powder. Its strong protein makes a dough that holds its shape through drying and boiling, which is why dried pasta and couscous rely on it. It also dusts pizza peels.
cards.origin: Italian semola, from Latin for fine flour
cards.notThis: Not cornmeal or polenta, though all three are yellow and gritty. Semolina is wheat, cornmeal is corn.
cards.line: Hand-rolled semolina cavatelli, tomato, basil

cards.gist: Long, flat ribbons of fresh egg pasta, the classic from Bologna
cards.guest: They're long, flat ribbons of fresh egg pasta from Bologna, classic with a slow meat ragu. Silky and tender, and the sauce clings to them.
cards.why: Egg and flour dough is rolled into thin sheets and cut into ribbons about 7 to 8 millimeters wide. The egg makes them rich and tender, and the rolled surface is porous, so a meaty sauce clings. Narrower than pappardelle, much like fettuccine.
cards.origin: Emilia-Romagna, from tagliare, Italian for to cut
cards.pairs: Ragu Bolognese, butter and parmesan, mushrooms, truffle
cards.notThis: Not pappardelle, which are about three times as wide. Tagliatelle are close to fettuccine, the Roman name.
cards.line: Tagliatelle Bolognese, aged parmesan

cards.gist: Plump, pearly short-grain Italian rice, the best known for risotto
cards.guest: It's the classic Italian risotto rice. The plump grains release lots of starch, so the dish turns rich and creamy.
cards.why: A superfino rice named for the town of Arborio in Piedmont. Its fat grains have a chalky white core and shed surface starch readily, which thickens the broth into a creamy sauce. It softens sooner than carnaroli, so timing matters.
cards.origin: Named for the town of Arborio, Vercelli, Piedmont
cards.notThis: Not carnaroli, the longer, firmer grain many chefs prefer. Arborio is rounder and turns soft sooner.
cards.line: Arborio risotto, spring peas, parmesan
cards.prompt: A superfino rice named for the town of __ in Piedmont. Its fat grains have a chalky white core and shed surface starch readily, which thickens the broth into a creamy sauce. It softens sooner than carnaroli, so timing matters.

cards.gist: Tiny steamed beads of rolled semolina from North Africa
cards.guest: It's tiny wheat pasta from North Africa, steamed until light and fluffy. It soaks up the broth of whatever stew it's served with.
cards.why: Durum semolina is sprinkled with water and rolled by hand or machine into tiny granules, then dried. Steamed, often over a simmering stew, the beads swell and fluff apart. Most sold today is precooked and only needs soaking in boiling liquid.
cards.origin: The Maghreb: Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia
cards.pairs: Tagine, lamb, merguez, seven vegetables, harissa
cards.notThis: Not a grain like bulgur or a seed like quinoa. It is pasta made from wheat. Pearl couscous is a larger, toasted pasta.
cards.line: Lamb tagine, apricot, saffron couscous

cards.gist: Green wheat roasted over fire, then rubbed clean and often cracked
cards.guest: It's young wheat picked green and roasted over fire, so it tastes a little smoky. It cooks up chewy and nutty, like a toasty cousin of bulgur.
cards.why: The wheat, usually durum, is cut while still green and soft, piled and set alight so the straw and chaff burn off while the moist kernels only char. The kernels are rubbed clean and often cracked. That early harvest and fire give a firm chew and a smoky, grassy flavor.
cards.origin: The Levant and Egypt; from Arabic farik, meaning rubbed
cards.pairs: Roast lamb, chicken, yogurt, herbs and pomegranate
cards.notThis: Not bulgur, which is ripe wheat parboiled, dried and cracked, with no smoke. Freekeh tastes of the fire.
cards.line: Freekeh salad, charred eggplant, herbs, yogurt

cards.gist: Long black seed of a North American lake grass, firm and nutty
cards.guest: It's the seed of a grass that grows in northern lakes, not true rice. It's chewy and nutty, with a toasty, almost tea-like flavor.
cards.why: It comes from Zizania, a water grass native to the Great Lakes, gathered by canoe by the Ojibwe, who call it manoomin. Most sold today is paddy grown in Minnesota and California. The hard dark bran coat keeps it chewy, and cooked grains split to show white inside.
cards.note: Takes 45 to 60 minutes to cook, so kitchens make it ahead. Split grains are a sign it is done.
cards.pairs: Duck, game birds, mushrooms, dried cranberries
cards.notThis: Not black rice, which is a true Asian rice whose dark color sits in its bran.
cards.line: Roast duck, wild rice, cherries, pan jus

cards.gist: Very wide, flat ribbons of fresh egg pasta, made for heavy meat sauces
cards.guest: They're wide, silky ribbons of fresh egg pasta. They're built to carry a rich, slow-cooked sauce, so every forkful gets plenty of it.
cards.why: Fresh egg dough is rolled thin and cut into ribbons about two to three centimeters wide. The width and the egg make them tender but sturdy, with lots of surface to hold a chunky braise. Tuscany serves them with wild boar, hare or duck ragu.
cards.origin: Tuscany, Italy; from pappare, to gobble up
cards.pairs: Wild boar, hare or duck ragu, mushrooms, braised short rib
cards.notThis: Not tagliatelle, which is the same egg dough cut about a third as wide.
cards.line: Pappardelle, wild boar ragu, pecorino

cards.gist: Square pillows of pasta, two sheets pressed together around a filling
cards.guest: They're little pillows of fresh pasta sealed around a filling, often ricotta or meat. Soft and rich inside, with a tender bite of pasta around it.
cards.why: A spoonful of filling goes on one sheet of fresh dough, a second sheet goes over it, and the pillows are pressed and cut apart. That gives a flat, sealed edge on every side. Ricotta and spinach is the classic, but meat, squash and cheese are common too.
cards.note: Fillings change by kitchen and by day. Check tonight's filling before describing it.
cards.pairs: Brown butter and sage, tomato sauce, parmesan
cards.notThis: Agnolotti fold one sheet over the filling and pinch, so they have a fold on one side.
cards.line: Ricotta ravioli, brown butter, sage

cards.gist: Small rings of stuffed egg pasta, twisted around a fingertip
cards.guest: They're little rings of fresh pasta, classically filled with pork and parmesan. In Bologna they come floating in a rich, clear broth.
cards.why: A tiny square of egg dough gets a dab of filling, is folded to a triangle, then wrapped around a fingertip and pinched into a ring. The Bologna filling is pork loin, prosciutto, mortadella and parmesan. Small and dense, they are meant for broth.
cards.origin: Bologna and Modena, Italy; a small tortello, from torta, a pie
cards.notThis: Not ravioli, which are flat sealed pillows. Tortelloni are bigger rings, often ricotta-filled.
cards.line: Tortellini in brodo, parmesan

cards.gist: Short semolina dough curls shaped like tiny split hot dog buns
cards.guest: They're little hand-rolled pasta curls from southern Italy, like tiny hot dog buns. Dense and chewy, and the hollow holds sauce.
cards.why: A rope of semolina and water dough is cut into short pieces, and each is pulled with a fingertip or a small wooden board so it curls around a hollow. Durum semolina and water give a firm, chewy bite, more like a dumpling than a noodle.
cards.origin: Molise and Puglia, Italy; from cavare, to hollow out
cards.pairs: Sausage and broccoli rabe, tomato sauce, ricotta
cards.notThis: Not gnocchi, which are soft potato dumplings, and not orecchiette, which are round cupped ears. These are short curls with a slit.
cards.line: Cavatelli, sausage, broccoli rabe, chili

cards.gist: Small cupped disks of semolina dough, thin in the middle
cards.guest: The name means little ears. They're small cupped pasta from Puglia, chewy at the rim and tender in the middle, and the cup scoops up sauce.
cards.why: Semolina and water dough is cut into small nubs, dragged across a board with a knife so each one curls, then flipped inside out over a thumb. That leaves a rough outside, a thin center and a thick rim, so one piece eats both tender and chewy.
cards.origin: Puglia, Italy; Italian for little ears
cards.pairs: Broccoli rabe, garlic, anchovy and chili; sausage
cards.notThis: Cavatelli are curled like a shell. These are round and domed like a small ear.
cards.line: Orecchiette, broccoli rabe, anchovy, chili

cards.gist: Thick garlic cream of olive oil beaten in drop by drop
cards.guest: It's a garlic sauce from the south of France, whipped with olive oil until it's thick and creamy. Great for dipping fries or spreading on a sandwich.
cards.why: Garlic is pounded to a paste and olive oil is whisked in slowly until it thickens like mayonnaise. Most kitchens use egg yolk to hold it, as mayonnaise does, though the oldest versions rely on garlic alone. Raw garlic gives it real heat and bite.
cards.note: Made with raw egg yolk in most kitchens, so ask whether yours is raw or pasteurized.
cards.origin: Provence and Catalonia, from the words for garlic and oil
cards.line: Crispy fries, smoked paprika aioli

cards.gist: Warm butter sauce of yolks, tarragon, shallot and vinegar
cards.guest: It's a warm, buttery sauce with tarragon and shallot, the classic partner for steak. Rich like hollandaise but with a tangy herb bite.
cards.why: A reduction of vinegar, shallot, tarragon and pepper is whisked with egg yolks over gentle heat, then butter goes in slowly until it turns thick and glossy. It is a child of hollandaise: the reduction and herbs give it tang and an anise note.
cards.pairs: Filet, steak frites, grilled fish, roast beef
cards.notThis: Not hollandaise, the same yolks and butter with lemon. This one is flecked green with tarragon.
cards.line: Filet mignon, pommes frites, béarnaise

cards.gist: Warm lemony sauce of egg yolks and melted butter
cards.guest: It's a warm, silky butter sauce brightened with lemon, the one on eggs Benedict. It's lovely over asparagus or fish too.
cards.why: Egg yolks and a little water or lemon are whisked over gentle heat, then melted butter goes in a little at a time. The yolks hold the butter as tiny droplets, so it turns thick and pale. One of the French mother sauces; béarnaise grows from it.
cards.note: The yolks are only gently warmed, never set firm. Ask the kitchen whether it uses pasteurized eggs.
cards.pairs: Eggs Benedict, asparagus, poached salmon, artichokes
cards.notThis: Not béarnaise, which adds tarragon and shallot, and not beurre blanc, a butter sauce built on wine and shallot.
cards.line: Eggs Benedict, Canadian bacon, hollandaise

cards.gist: Fat and liquid beaten into one smooth, even mix
cards.guest: It means the sauce is whisked or blended so the oil and the liquid stay together, which makes it silky and rich on the tongue.
cards.why: Oil and water separate, but beaten hard they break into droplets, and an emulsifier such as egg yolk or mustard keeps them apart. Mayonnaise, hollandaise and vinaigrette all work this way. Too hot, too cold or too much fat and it breaks into a greasy puddle.
cards.origin: Latin emulgere, to milk out: milk is itself one
cards.line: Seared scallops, brown butter emulsion, peas

cards.gist: Thin, glossy sauce made from roast meat's own juices, cooked down
cards.guest: It's the natural juices from the roast, cooked down into a light, glossy sauce. All the flavor of the meat without the heaviness of gravy.
cards.why: Drippings left in the roasting pan are loosened with stock or wine and simmered down, then strained. It is left thin or only lightly thickened, so it pours like broth but tastes deep. Any roast can make one: lamb, chicken, pork, veal or beef.
cards.origin: French for juice; au jus means served with its own juices
cards.notThis: Not gravy, which is thickened much further, and not demi-glace, a far thicker veal reduction.
cards.line: Roast lamb loin, fondant potato, rosemary jus

cards.gist: Oil whisked with vinegar or citrus, held with mustard
cards.guest: It's a light dressing of good oil and vinegar with a little mustard and shallot. Bright and tangy, it lets the greens taste like themselves.
cards.why: The classic ratio is about three parts oil to one of vinegar. Whisked hard, the vinegar breaks into droplets in the oil, and mustard helps them stay put, but it still separates on standing, so it gets a shake. Beyond salad it dresses leeks, fish and grains.
cards.origin: French, from vinaigre, vinegar
cards.line: Little gems, radish, sherry vinaigrette

cards.gist: Minced shallot and black pepper steeped in vinegar
cards.guest: It's a sharp little sauce of shallot, cracked pepper and vinegar for the oysters. A few drops brighten the brine without covering it.
cards.why: Shallot is minced fine and steeped in red wine or champagne vinegar with coarsely cracked black pepper. It is thinner and sharper than any salad dressing, so it cuts the oyster's salt and richness instead of masking it.
cards.origin: French for coarsely cracked pepper, the heart of the sauce
cards.pairs: Raw oysters on the half shell, clams, crudo
cards.line: East Coast oysters, champagne mignonette, lemon

cards.gist: Caramelized sugar cooked with vinegar into a syrup
cards.guest: It's a sweet and tangy glaze made from caramel and vinegar, often with fruit. It's there to cut the richness of the meat.
cards.why: Sugar is cooked to caramel, then vinegar goes in and it simmers to a syrup, often with fruit or stock. The caramel brings depth, the vinegar brings snap, and together they cut through rich, fatty meats. The base of classic duck with orange.
cards.pairs: Duck breast, pork belly, foie gras, stone fruit
cards.notThis: Not agrodolce, the Italian sweet-sour that is often chunky with onion or raisins. This one is a smooth syrup.
cards.line: Seared duck breast, cherry gastrique, parsnip

cards.gist: Smooth, strained purée of fruit or vegetable, served as a sauce
cards.guest: It's ripe fruit, or sometimes a vegetable, blended and strained into a smooth, pourable sauce. It tastes like the fruit itself, only silkier.
cards.why: Fruit such as raspberry or mango, or a vegetable such as roasted red pepper, is blended, lightly sweetened and pushed through a fine sieve to catch seeds and skins. Raw or barely cooked and thickened by its own pulp, it tastes fresh, not jammy.
cards.origin: French, from couler, to flow or to strain
cards.pairs: Cheesecake, panna cotta, chocolate cake, ice cream
cards.notThis: Not a compote, which is fruit cooked in soft chunks. This is blended and strained perfectly smooth.
cards.line: Vanilla cheesecake, raspberry coulis, mint

cards.gist: Rich meat stock made crystal clear by a raft of egg white
cards.guest: It's a rich broth made crystal clear with egg white. You can see the bottom of the bowl, yet every spoonful tastes of long-simmered meat.
cards.why: A strong stock is whisked cold with egg whites, lean ground meat and chopped vegetables, then heated gently. The whites set into a floating raft that traps the cloudy particles while the meat adds flavor. The broth is ladled out through a hole in the raft and strained.
cards.origin: French for completed, a stock taken to its finish
cards.notThis: Not plain broth or stock, which stays cloudy. Clarity is the test: a true one is see-through.
cards.line: Oxtail consommé, root vegetables, chervil

cards.gist: Cold butter whisked into a reduction of wine and shallot
cards.guest: It's a warm butter sauce sharpened with white wine and shallot. Silky and rich with a bright finish, and a classic with fish and scallops.
cards.why: White wine and vinegar are boiled down with minced shallot to a few spoonfuls, then cold butter is whisked in piece by piece. Kept just warm, the butter stays suspended as an emulsion, so the sauce eats creamy rather than oily and the acid cuts the richness.
cards.note: Fragile. Too hot and it splits into oil, too cold and it sets, so kitchens make it near service and hold it just warm.
cards.origin: French for white butter, from the Loire Valley near Nantes
cards.notThis: Not hollandaise, which is thickened with egg yolk. This is butter whisked into a wine reduction.
cards.line: Seared scallops, beurre blanc, spring peas

cards.gist: Glossy brown sauce base of roasted veal stock reduced by half
cards.guest: It's a deeply reduced meat sauce, classically veal, glossy and rich and the backbone of a great steak sauce. Think of the best gravy you've had, concentrated.
cards.why: Veal bones and vegetables are roasted and simmered for hours into brown stock, which is then reduced by about half, classically with a roux-thickened brown sauce. Gelatin from the bones gives body and shine, and the long reduction concentrates roasted, meaty flavor.
cards.origin: French for half glaze, halfway between a sauce and a glaze
cards.pairs: Steak, veal chop, short rib, and the base of bordelaise
cards.notThis: Not jus, the thin, unthickened pan juice. This is thicker and glossier and coats a spoon.
cards.line: Grilled veal chop, potato purée, demi-glace

cards.gist: Pale mother sauce of light stock thickened with butter and flour
cards.guest: It's a silky sauce made from chicken or fish broth, thickened lightly. Mild and savory, it lets delicate fish or chicken taste like themselves.
cards.why: Butter and flour are cooked to a pale roux, then light stock from chicken, veal or fish is whisked in and simmered until smooth. Finished with cream it becomes sauce suprême, and with wine and cream a white wine sauce for fish.
cards.note: On a menu the word can also name a silky puréed soup, as in mushroom velouté.
cards.origin: French for velvety, one of the five mother sauces
cards.notThis: Not béchamel, which is made with milk. This is built on stock, so it tastes savory, not milky.
cards.line: Poached halibut, mussel velouté, leeks

cards.gist: Hot milk thickened with butter and flour, the white base
cards.guest: It's a creamy white sauce of milk thickened with butter and flour. It's what makes a classic lasagna, a gratin or a croque monsieur so rich.
cards.why: Butter and flour are cooked briefly without browning, then hot milk is whisked in and simmered until thick and smooth, often seasoned with nutmeg. Add cheese and it becomes Mornay, the sauce behind many gratins and baked macaroni. It tastes mild, milky and gentle.
cards.origin: French, traditionally named for Louis de Béchameil, steward to Louis XIV
cards.pairs: Lasagna, croque monsieur, gratins, moussaka
cards.notThis: Not velouté, which thickens light stock the same way. This one is built on milk, so it is paler and milkier.
cards.line: Croque monsieur, ham, gruyère, béchamel

cards.gist: Cold mayonnaise sauce sharpened with pickles, capers and mustard
cards.guest: It's a tangy, creamy cold sauce, mayonnaise sharpened with mustard, pickles and herbs. It's great with anything fried, especially crab cakes.
cards.why: Most start with mayonnaise, an emulsion of egg yolk and oil, then take chopped pickles, capers, herbs and mustard. The French version is pale and herby. The Louisiana one is often pink or orange with Creole mustard, paprika, hot sauce and horseradish, and bolder.
cards.note: House-made versions are often whisked from raw egg yolk. Ask the kitchen whether theirs uses pasteurized egg.
cards.pairs: Crab cakes, fried shrimp, po' boys, celery root salad
cards.notThis: Not tartar sauce, though close. It is usually more mustardy and herby, and in Louisiana spicier and pinker.
cards.line: Crab cakes, Creole remoulade, pickled okra

cards.gist: Raw Argentine sauce of parsley, garlic, oil and vinegar
cards.guest: It's Argentina's steak sauce, chopped parsley and garlic in oil and vinegar with a little chili. Bright and sharp, it cuts through rich grilled meat.
cards.why: Parsley, garlic and dried oregano are chopped, usually by hand rather than blended, and loosened with oil, red wine vinegar and red pepper flakes. Raw garlic and vinegar make it sharp enough to cut fat, which is why it sits beside grilled beef at an Argentine asado.
cards.origin: Argentina and Uruguay, the table sauce of the asado grill
cards.notThis: Not pesto or Italian salsa verde. This is loose, vinegar-sharp and flecked with oregano and chili.
cards.line: Wood-grilled skirt steak, chimichurri, crispy potatoes

cards.gist: Chopped parsley sauce sharpened with capers, anchovy and vinegar
cards.guest: It's a bright Italian green sauce of chopped parsley, capers, anchovy and good olive oil. It wakes up rich meats and grilled fish.
cards.why: The herbs are chopped by hand rather than blended, loosened with olive oil and sharpened with vinegar or lemon. Capers and anchovy add salt and savory depth without tasting fishy, and the acid cuts through fatty meat. It is served at room temperature, never cooked.
cards.origin: Italian for green sauce, classic beside the boiled meats of Piedmont
cards.notThis: Not chimichurri, which leans on oregano and chili and skips the capers. Mexican salsa verde is a tomatillo salsa.
cards.line: Grilled swordfish, salsa verde, charred lemon

cards.gist: Pounded basil sauce with pine nuts, garlic, hard cheese and oil
cards.guest: It's the classic basil sauce from Genoa, made with pine nuts, garlic, Parmesan and olive oil. Fresh, green and nutty, it clings to pasta.
cards.why: The name comes from the Italian for to pound, as in a mortar and pestle. Crushing the leaves bursts their oils instead of slicing them, so the sauce is fragrant and glossy. Cheese and nuts give it body, so it coats pasta the way a cream sauce would.
cards.note: Cut basil darkens in air, so a dull top layer is normal. Kitchens often seal it under a film of oil.
cards.origin: Genoa in Liguria, from pestare, Italian for to pound
cards.pairs: Trofie or trenette with green beans and potato, minestrone
cards.line: Trofie, basil pesto, green beans, potato

cards.gist: Catalan sauce of dried red peppers, roasted tomato, nuts and bread
cards.guest: It's a Catalan sauce of dried sweet red peppers and roasted tomato, ground with toasted almonds and garlic. Earthy, nutty and a little sweet.
cards.why: Dried sweet peppers, traditionally the small round ñora, are soaked and ground with roasted tomato and garlic, then thickened with toasted almonds or hazelnuts and fried bread. The nuts and bread make it thick and spoonable, and a splash of vinegar keeps it bright.
cards.origin: Tarragona on the Catalan coast, said to come from its fishermen
cards.pairs: Grilled spring onions and leeks, grilled fish, potatoes
cards.line: Grilled leeks, romesco, toasted hazelnuts

cards.gist: Liquid simmered from bones and aromatics, the base under sauces
cards.guest: It's the kitchen's foundation, bones and vegetables simmered slowly in water into a rich liquid. It's what gives sauces and soups their depth.
cards.why: Bones and vegetables simmer gently in water for hours, or under an hour for fish. Collagen in the bones melts into gelatin, which gives stock body and makes it set when cold. Roasting the bones first makes brown stock, deeper in color and flavor, for dark sauces.
cards.note: Kitchens usually leave it unsalted, because it gets reduced into sauces and salt would concentrate.
cards.notThis: Not broth, which is made from meat and seasoned to drink. Stock is a building block, rarely served on its own.
cards.line: Steamed clams, fish stock, white wine, grilled bread
cards.prompt: Bones and vegetables simmer gently in water for hours, or under an hour for fish. Collagen in the bones melts into gelatin, which gives __ body and makes it set when cold. Roasting the bones first makes brown __, deeper in color and flavor, for dark sauces.

cards.gist: Italian sweet-sour sauce of vinegar, sugar, raisins and onion
cards.guest: It's the Italian take on sweet and sour, vinegar and sugar or honey cooked down, often with raisins and onions. It makes rich meats and vegetables pop.
cards.why: Vinegar is cooked with sugar or honey until syrupy, and in Sicily raisins, pine nuts and onions often go in. The sweetness rounds off the vinegar's edge, so it cuts through fat without puckering, which is why it lands on duck, pork, rabbit and squash.
cards.origin: Italian for sour-sweet, strongest in Sicilian and Roman cooking
cards.notThis: Not gastrique, the smooth French sauce base of caramelized sugar and vinegar. Agrodolce is chunkier and often holds fruit and onion.
cards.line: Roast duck breast, cherry agrodolce, farro

cards.gist: Raw beef, or sometimes fish, sliced paper thin to cover the plate
cards.guest: It's raw beef sliced so thin you can almost see through it, dressed with olive oil, lemon and shaved Parmesan. Light, silky and bright.
cards.why: Chilled lean beef, often tenderloin, is sliced paper thin or pounded flat between sheets, so the raw meat melts on the tongue instead of chewing. Harry's Bar in Venice made it around 1950 with a thin mayonnaise sauce. Menus now use the word for any thin raw slice.
cards.origin: Harry's Bar, Venice, named for the painter Vittore Carpaccio and his reds
cards.pairs: Arugula, shaved Parmesan, capers, lemon, olive oil
cards.notThis: Not tartare, which is raw meat chopped fine, and not bresaola, which is cured. Carpaccio is fresh, raw and sliced flat.
cards.line: Beef carpaccio, arugula, Parmesan, lemon oil

cards.gist: Raw beef or fish chopped fine by knife, seasoned and served in a mound
cards.guest: It's raw beef chopped fine by hand and mixed with capers, shallot and mustard, often with an egg yolk on top. Rich, tender and savory, served with toast or fries.
cards.why: The meat is cut with a knife, not ground, so it stays in tiny tender pieces rather than a paste. Salty capers, sharp shallot, mustard and a raw yolk season and bind it. Tuna and salmon versions use the same method with lighter dressings, often soy and citrus.
cards.note: The yolk is served raw along with the meat.
cards.pairs: Frites, toasted baguette, cornichons, a raw egg yolk
cards.notThis: Not carpaccio, which is sliced whole and flat. Tartare is chopped into small pieces and piled up.
cards.line: Hand-cut beef tartare, egg yolk, capers, frites

cards.gist: Thick open egg dish with its fillings set right in, cut into wedges
cards.guest: It's an Italian egg dish, thick and open like a crustless pie, with the vegetables and cheese cooked right into the eggs. Served in wedges, warm or at room temperature.
cards.why: Beaten eggs are poured over the fillings in a pan and cooked gently until the bottom sets, then finished in the oven or flipped. Slow heat gives an even, tender slice. An omelette is cooked fast and folded, and a quiche sits in pastry with cream.
cards.origin: Italian, from friggere, to fry
cards.pairs: Green salad, roasted peppers, crusty bread
cards.line: Frittata of spring onion, ricotta and herbs

cards.gist: Slow-simmered stew of meat, fish or vegetables in a thick sauce
cards.guest: It's a slow-simmered stew, the meat or vegetables cooked gently in a rich sauce until tender. Deep, savory and made for spooning over something soft.
cards.why: Pieces of meat or vegetables are browned, then simmered low in stock or wine until the connective tissue relaxes and the liquid reduces to a thick, glossy sauce. It is braising in small pieces. The Italian cousin, ragù, is usually a meat sauce for pasta.
cards.origin: French ragoût, from ragoûter, to revive the appetite
cards.pairs: Polenta, mashed potato, egg noodles, crusty bread
cards.line: Lamb ragout, white beans, gremolata

cards.gist: Very fresh raw fish dressed simply, Italian style, as it goes out
cards.guest: It's raw fish sliced thin and dressed at the last second with good olive oil, citrus and sea salt. Clean, cool and delicate, the fish is the whole point.
cards.why: Italian for raw. Very fresh fish or shellfish is sliced and dressed moments before it goes out, so the acid has no time to firm it and the flesh stays soft and glossy. Think sashimi with Italian seasoning, or ceviche without the long soak.
cards.note: Served raw and dressed at the pass, so run it out right away.
cards.pairs: Olive oil, lemon, flaky salt, chili, shaved fennel
cards.notThis: Not ceviche, which sits in lime juice until the fish turns opaque. Crudo is dressed at the last moment and stays glossy.
cards.line: Hamachi crudo, blood orange, chili, olive oil

cards.gist: Raw fish soaked in lime juice until it firms and turns opaque
cards.guest: It's raw fish marinated in fresh lime juice with red onion, chili and cilantro. The lime firms it and makes it bright, tangy and refreshing.
cards.why: Acid in lime juice unwinds the fish's proteins the way heat does, so the flesh turns white and firm in minutes, though nothing is cooked. It is Peru's national dish, and the tangy, spicy liquid left in the bowl is called leche de tigre, tiger's milk.
cards.note: The lime changes the texture but does not cook it. Treat it as raw fish.
cards.pairs: Sweet potato, boiled corn, crunchy toasted corn, red onion
cards.notThis: Not crudo, which is raw fish dressed with oil at the last second, and not escabeche, which is cooked first. Ceviche soaks raw in lime.
cards.line: Peruvian ceviche, leche de tigre, sweet potato, corn

cards.gist: Salmon cured raw under salt, sugar and dill, then sliced thin
cards.guest: It's Scandinavian salmon cured for a few days with salt, sugar and fresh dill, never smoked. Silky, sweet and herby, usually with a mustard dill sauce.
cards.why: A side of salmon is packed in salt, sugar and dill and pressed in the fridge for two to three days. Salt draws out water and firms the flesh while sugar keeps it tender, so it slices like silk. Smoked salmon is cured, then smoked, so it tastes of wood.
cards.note: Cured but never cooked, so it is served raw.
cards.origin: Swedish, literally grave salmon, once buried in sand to cure
cards.notThis: Not smoked salmon. Gravlax is cured with no smoke, so it is paler, sweeter and tastes of dill, not wood.
cards.line: House gravlax, mustard dill sauce, rye crisps

cards.gist: Fish or beef seared for seconds, rare inside, then sliced and dressed
cards.guest: It's tuna or beef seared for just a few seconds over high heat, so the edge is cooked and the center stays rare. Sliced thin with a bright citrus soy sauce.
cards.why: The meat is kissed by a very hot flame or pan, then often plunged into ice water to stop the cooking, leaving a thin browned rim around a cool raw center. It began in Kochi with bonito seared over burning straw. The name means pounded, from patting in the garnish.
cards.note: Seared outside only. The center is served raw by design. Ask the kitchen before promising more heat.
cards.pairs: Ponzu, scallion, grated ginger, garlic chips, sesame
cards.line: Seared tuna tataki, ponzu, scallion, sesame

cards.gist: Fish or meat cooked first, then left to cool in a spiced vinegar
cards.guest: It's fish that's cooked, then left to marinate in a warm, spiced vinegar, often served cool. Bright, tangy and tender, like a gentle pickle.
cards.why: The fish or meat is fried or poached first, then covered in hot vinegar and oil with garlic, bay, onion and spices. As it rests, the acid seasons and firms the flesh. Think a gentle pickle, served cool in Spain and often hot in the Philippines.
cards.origin: Spain, from an Arabic word for a vinegar stew; now across Latin America and the Philippines
cards.notThis: Not ceviche, which is raw fish cured in citrus. Escabeche is always cooked before it meets the vinegar.
cards.line: Mackerel escabeche, pickled shallot, grilled bread

cards.gist: Dish baked in a shallow pan until its top forms a browned crust
cards.guest: It's baked in a shallow dish until the top turns golden and crisp. The classic is thin sliced potatoes baked soft in cream.
cards.why: The word means the crust. A wide, shallow dish gives lots of surface, so the top browns under high heat while the inside turns tender and creamy. Cheese or breadcrumbs help it brown, but the classic potato version from the Dauphine skips cheese entirely.
cards.origin: French, from gratter, to scrape: the crust once scraped from the pan
cards.pairs: Roast lamb, steak, roast chicken
cards.line: Potato gratin, gruyère, thyme

cards.gist: Creamy filling shaped into a small log, breaded and deep-fried
cards.guest: It's a little breaded, fried bite with a crisp shell and a soft, creamy middle. The filling is often ham, fish or cheese in a silky white sauce.
cards.why: A filling of mashed potato or a thick white sauce folded with ham, fish or cheese is chilled until firm, shaped, rolled in flour, egg and crumbs, then fried. The crust sets fast and the inside turns molten, so it eats crunchy then creamy.
cards.note: The center holds heat far longer than the shell. Warn guests the first bite runs hot.
cards.origin: French, from croquer, to crunch; in Spain croqueta
cards.line: Jamón croquettes, saffron aioli

cards.gist: Thin flat layer spread with filling, rolled into a spiral and sliced
cards.guest: It's thin meat or cake rolled around a filling, then sliced so every piece shows a pretty spiral. A savory one is often pork or chicken rolled with herbs and greens.
cards.why: Meat is pounded or butterflied thin, or a sponge cake baked in a flat sheet, then spread with filling and rolled tight, the meat ones tied. Rolling means every slice gets the filling and cooks evenly. The same idea makes a jelly roll or a Yule log.
cards.origin: French, from rouler, to roll
cards.notThis: Not a ballotine, which is a boned bird or leg stuffed and reshaped. A roulade starts as a flat sheet of anything, even cake.
cards.line: Pork roulade, braised greens, mustard jus

cards.gist: Poultry leg or bird with the bones removed, stuffed and rolled tight
cards.guest: It's usually a chicken leg or a whole bird with the bones taken out, filled with a savory stuffing and rolled. Every slice is juicy meat around a rich center.
cards.why: The cook bones the bird or leg while keeping the skin whole, fills it with a forcemeat of ground meat, herbs and cream, then rolls and ties it. Poached or roasted, the skin holds the juices in, so it slices clean and stays moist, a boneless roast in miniature.
cards.origin: French, from ballot, a small bundle
cards.notThis: Not a roulade, which rolls a flat sheet of anything. A ballotine is a boned bird, leg or fish rebuilt around stuffing.
cards.line: Chicken ballotine, mushroom farce, pan jus

cards.gist: Slow-baked casserole of white beans, duck confit, sausage and pork
cards.guest: It's a slow-baked French casserole of white beans with slow-cooked duck, garlic sausage and pork. Hearty and rich, with a golden crust.
cards.why: Dried white beans are simmered with pork and aromatics, layered with duck or goose confit and garlicky sausage, then baked for hours. The beans soak up the fat and turn creamy while a crust forms on top, which cooks break and push under to thicken the pot.
cards.origin: Languedoc, France; named for the cassole, its earthenware pot
cards.pairs: Red wine from southwest France, green salad
cards.line: Duck cassoulet, garlic sausage, pork belly

cards.gist: Marseille stew of several fish in a saffron and fennel broth
cards.guest: It's the famous fish stew of Marseille, several kinds of fish in a golden saffron broth, with toast and a garlicky sauce to float on top.
cards.why: Rockfish and other catch are boiled hard in olive oil, tomato, fennel, orange peel and saffron, so the oil emulsifies into a rich, silky broth. It is served with toasted bread and rouille, a garlic and saffron mayonnaise stirred into the broth.
cards.note: Whole or bone-in fish may be used. Ask the kitchen before promising a guest no bones.
cards.origin: Marseille, France; from bouillir and abaisser, to boil then lower the heat
cards.pairs: Rouille, toasted bread, dry rosé
cards.line: Bouillabaisse, rockfish, mussels, rouille, crouton

cards.gist: Fish or vegetables sealed in a parchment packet to steam in the oven
cards.guest: It's fish baked sealed inside a parchment paper pouch, so it steams in its own juices. When the pouch is cut open, you get all the aroma.
cards.why: Fish, herbs, vegetables and a splash of wine or butter are sealed in folded parchment and baked. The trapped moisture turns to steam, cooking the food gently without drying it and keeping every drop of flavor in the packet. Delicate fish suits it best.
cards.origin: French, in paper; a papillote was a paper frill or curl paper
cards.notThis: Not baked in pastry. The wrap is parchment or foil, cut open and set aside, not eaten.
cards.line: Halibut en papillote, fennel, lemon, white wine

cards.gist: Floured fish fried in butter, dressed only in brown butter and lemon
cards.guest: It's fish dusted in flour and pan-fried in butter, then finished with nutty browned butter, lemon and parsley. Simple, crisp-edged and rich.
cards.why: The fish is dredged in flour and fried in butter, so the flour browns into a thin golden skin that keeps delicate flesh moist. The butter is cooked on until it smells of hazelnuts, then sharpened with lemon and parsley. Think lemon-butter fish, toastier.
cards.note: Sole may come whole on the bone and be filleted tableside, so small bones are possible.
cards.origin: French for the miller's wife, named for the flour dusting
cards.pairs: Sole, trout, boiled potatoes, green beans, spinach
cards.notThis: Not beurre blanc, a creamy white wine butter sauce. This butter is browned and nutty, not pale.
cards.line: Dover sole meunière, brown butter, lemon, parsley

cards.gist: Pan-fried fish topped with toasted sliced almonds in browned butter
cards.guest: It means with almonds. The fish is pan-fried in butter and topped with toasted sliced almonds in a nutty brown butter with lemon.
cards.why: It builds on the classic floured, butter-fried fish. Sliced almonds are toasted in the pan butter as it browns, so almond and butter pick up the same roasted flavor, then lemon cuts the richness. You get crunch on top of soft, flaky fish.
cards.origin: French, meaning made with almonds; trout is the classic, a New Orleans staple
cards.pairs: Trout, green beans, rice, lemon, parsley
cards.line: Trout amandine, brown butter, lemon, haricots verts

cards.gist: Squares of yeasted dough, deep-fried and buried in powdered sugar
cards.guest: They're little squares of sweet dough fried until they puff up hollow, then heaped with powdered sugar. Best eaten hot.
cards.why: A soft, lightly sweet yeast dough is rolled thin, cut into squares and dropped into hot oil. Steam puffs each one into a pillow with a crisp shell and an airy, hollow middle. Lighter and less sweet than a doughnut, so the sugar on top does most of the work.
cards.origin: French word for fritter, made famous in New Orleans
cards.pairs: Chicory coffee, café au lait, chocolate or caramel dipping sauce
cards.line: Warm beignets, powdered sugar, chicory crème anglaise

cards.gist: Soft, golden French loaf enriched with plenty of eggs and butter
cards.guest: It's a French bread made rich with eggs and butter, so it's soft, golden and a little sweet. Almost halfway between bread and cake.
cards.why: The dough is kneaded first, then butter is worked in bit by bit, often a third or more of the flour's weight, with plenty of egg. The fat and yolk make a tender, cottony crumb and a deep brown crust. It toasts fast, which is why it carries burgers and French toast.
cards.pairs: Burgers, lobster rolls, French toast, foie gras, jam and coffee
cards.line: Toasted brioche, foie gras torchon, fig jam

cards.gist: Thick, dimpled Italian flatbread baked in a pan pooled with olive oil
cards.guest: It's an Italian flatbread baked in lots of olive oil, crisp on the bottom and soft inside, usually topped with salt and rosemary.
cards.why: A wet yeast dough is pressed into a well-oiled pan and dimpled with fingertips so oil and salt pool in the holes. The oil fries the base and edges crisp while the thick middle stays open and springy. Taller and softer than pizza, and served as bread.
cards.origin: Italy, famed in Liguria. Latin for hearth
cards.pairs: Olive oil, cured meats, soft cheese, sandwiches, antipasti
cards.line: Warm rosemary focaccia, whipped ricotta, sea salt

cards.gist: Tangy bread raised by a living starter of wild yeast and bacteria
cards.guest: It's bread raised with a natural starter instead of packaged yeast, which gives it a gentle tang, a chewy crumb and a crackly crust.
cards.why: A starter is flour and water kept alive for years, full of wild yeasts that lift the dough and bacteria that make lactic and acetic acid. The slow rise builds the tang, a chewy, open crumb and a thick crust, and the acid helps the loaf keep longer than a quick yeast bread.
cards.origin: Ancient method, famous in San Francisco since the Gold Rush
cards.pairs: Cultured butter, olive oil, soups, toast, grilled cheese
cards.line: Grilled sourdough, cultured butter, flaky salt

cards.gist: Pair of smooth pastel almond meringue shells joined by a filling
cards.guest: It's a little French sandwich cookie of almond meringue, crisp outside and chewy inside, filled with ganache, buttercream or jam.
cards.why: Almond flour and sugar are folded into whipped egg whites, piped into rounds and rested until a skin forms, so they bake with a smooth dome and a ruffled foot. Sandwiched and left overnight, the filling softens the shells into that crisp, then chewy bite.
cards.origin: France, perfected in Paris pastry shops
cards.notThis: Not a macaroon, the single craggy mound of coconut. A macaron is smooth, round and filled.
cards.line: Pistachio and raspberry macarons

cards.gist: Craggy, chewy mound of sweetened shredded coconut and egg white
cards.guest: It's a chewy coconut cookie, toasty on the outside and soft in the middle, often with the bottom dipped in chocolate.
cards.why: Shredded coconut is bound with egg white and sugar, sometimes condensed milk, then scooped into mounds and baked until the peaks brown. The sugary whites set around the coconut, so it eats dense, moist and chewy, closer to candy than to a crisp cookie.
cards.origin: From Italian maccarone, a paste. In America it means coconut
cards.notThis: Not a macaron, the smooth filled almond sandwich. A macaroon is one rough, chewy coconut mound.
cards.line: Chocolate-dipped coconut macaroons, sea salt

cards.gist: Egg whites whipped stiff with sugar, then baked crisp or torched soft
cards.guest: It's egg whites whipped with sugar into a glossy foam. Baked, it turns crisp and melts away, and toasted on a pie it stays soft like marshmallow.
cards.why: Whipping unfolds the white's proteins around air bubbles, and sugar holds the foam firm. Baked low and slow it dries crisp and airy; browned fast on a pie or baked Alaska it stays soft inside. Swiss and Italian styles heat the whites as they whip, for a denser, glossier foam.
cards.note: A soft, torched topping can be only lightly cooked inside. Ask the kitchen which style it is.
cards.pairs: Lemon curd, berries, whipped cream, pie, baked Alaska
cards.line: Lemon tart, torched meringue, blackberry

cards.gist: Shallow open pastry shell with straight sides, filled and unmolded
cards.guest: It's a crisp, buttery pastry shell with no lid, filled with something like lemon curd, fruit or chocolate. Think of a pie's more elegant cousin.
cards.why: A short, buttery dough is pressed into a shallow ring with straight, often fluted sides, often baked empty first so it stays crisp, then filled. It stands on its own out of the pan, so each slice is mostly filling over a thin, snappy crust, unlike a deep, soft pie.
cards.pairs: Lemon curd, fresh berries, chocolate ganache, crème fraîche
cards.notThis: Not a torte, which is a rich cake, or a galette, which is folded free-form by hand with no pan.
cards.line: Lemon tart, raspberries, crème fraîche

cards.gist: Dense, rich European cake, often with ground nuts in the batter
cards.guest: It's a rich European-style cake, either one dense round or thin layers with a filling. Denser than a sponge, and a little goes a long way.
cards.why: German and Austrian bakers often build tortes from thin layers stacked with buttercream, jam or chocolate, or bake one dense round. Many swap part of the flour for ground nuts or crumbs, making them moist, dense and nutty. Compare Dobos torte to a light American layer cake.
cards.origin: German and Austrian, via Italian torta, a round cake or loaf
cards.notThis: Not a tart, which is a pastry shell holding a filling. A torte is dense cake, whether in one layer or several.
cards.line: Hazelnut torte, espresso cream, candied orange
cards.prompt: German and Austrian bakers often build __ from thin layers stacked with buttercream, jam or chocolate, or bake one dense round. Many swap part of the flour for ground nuts or crumbs, making them moist, dense and nutty. Compare Dobos __ to a light American layer cake.

cards.gist: Egg dough cooked on the stove, then baked into hollow shells to fill
cards.guest: It's the light, eggy dough behind cream puffs and eclairs. It bakes up crisp outside and hollow inside, ready to be filled with cream or something savory.
cards.why: Butter, water and flour are cooked in a pot into a paste, then eggs are beaten in. In the oven the water turns to steam and puffs each piece into a hollow shell that the eggs set firm. No yeast and no layers, unlike croissant or puff pastry dough.
cards.origin: French, choux means cabbages, for the knobbly look of the baked puffs
cards.notThis: Not puff pastry, which is flaky folded layers, and not pâté, the meat spread. Pâte just means dough.
cards.line: Warm choux puffs, vanilla cream, chocolate sauce

cards.gist: Unyeasted dough folded around butter into hundreds of flaky layers
cards.guest: It's the buttery, shattering pastry you get in a napoleon or a beef Wellington. Hundreds of paper-thin layers that crackle when you cut in.
cards.why: A block of butter is wrapped in plain dough, then rolled and folded again and again until there are hundreds of alternating layers. In the oven the water in the butter turns to steam and pushes the layers apart. Croissant dough is built the same way but adds yeast.
cards.origin: French pâte feuilletée, leafed dough, for its layers like pages
cards.notThis: Not choux, the eggy dough of cream puffs. Puff shatters into flakes, choux bakes into hollow shells.
cards.line: Mushroom and leek in puff pastry, Madeira sauce

cards.gist: Fruit baked in a sweet eggy batter that sets like a soft flan
cards.guest: It's a rustic French dessert of fruit, classically cherries, baked in a sweet custardy batter. Somewhere between a pancake and a flan, best served warm.
cards.why: Fruit goes into a buttered dish and a thin pancake-style batter of eggs, milk, sugar and a little flour is poured over. It bakes into a soft, puffed, custardy cake that sinks as it cools. With fruit other than cherries the French call it a flognarde.
cards.note: Traditional versions leave the cherry pits in for flavor. Ask the kitchen, and warn the guest if they are there.
cards.origin: Limousin, central France, from an old word meaning to fill
cards.line: Warm cherry clafoutis, crème fraîche

cards.gist: French flat round: a free-form folded-edge pie, or a buckwheat crepe
cards.guest: It's a rustic French pie baked free-form, with the crust folded up over the filling. In Brittany the same word means a savory buckwheat crepe.
cards.why: The word means a flat round cake. The dessert kind is dough rolled out, piled with fruit and its edges folded in, baked flat on a sheet with no tart ring, so it browns crisp all round. The Breton kind is a thin buckwheat crepe, often filled with ham, egg and cheese.
cards.origin: French, from galet, a smooth flat pebble
cards.notThis: Not a tart, which is baked in a fluted pan with straight sides. A galette is shaped by hand.
cards.line: Rustic plum galette, vanilla ice cream

cards.gist: Crisp meringue shell with a soft center, heaped with cream and fruit
cards.guest: It's a meringue cake that's crisp on the outside and soft like marshmallow inside, topped with whipped cream and fresh fruit. Light, sweet and tart at once.
cards.why: Egg whites are whipped with sugar, often with a little cornstarch and vinegar, then baked low and slow. The outside dries to a crisp shell while the center stays soft and chewy. Cream and sharp fruit like passion fruit cut the sweetness.
cards.note: Topped just before it goes out. Cream softens the shell, so it should not sit at the pass.
cards.origin: Australia and New Zealand, both claim it, named for ballerina Anna Pavlova
cards.line: Pavlova, passion fruit, berries, whipped cream

cards.gist: Baked egg dish lifted by whipped whites, served puffed and hot
cards.guest: It's a baked egg dish, savory with cheese or sweet with chocolate, that rises tall and airy around a soft, creamy middle. Made to order, and worth the wait.
cards.why: A thick base, cheese sauce for savory or pastry cream or fruit for sweet, is folded with beaten egg whites. In the oven the air and steam expand and push it up the straight sides of the dish. As it cools the air contracts, so it starts to fall within minutes.
cards.note: Takes about 20 minutes and falls fast, so warn the guest when they order.
cards.origin: French, souffler means to blow or puff up
cards.notThis: Not a mousse, which is set cold in the fridge. A hot soufflé is baked, and a frozen one is really a mousse.
cards.line: Gruyère soufflé, frisée, sherry vinaigrette

cards.gist: Pourable vanilla sauce of yolks and milk, stirred until it coats a spoon
cards.guest: It's a warm or cool vanilla custard sauce, silky and pourable, spooned around the plate. Think melted vanilla ice cream, only a little lighter.
cards.why: Egg yolks, sugar and milk are stirred over low heat until the yolks thicken it just enough to coat a spoon, about 82 C (180 F). There is no starch, so it stays a sauce and never sets. Churned in a machine, the same base becomes ice cream.
cards.origin: French for English cream, the classic French pouring custard
cards.notThis: Not pastry cream, which is thickened with starch and holds its shape. This one pours.
cards.line: Warm chocolate cake, crème anglaise, raspberries

cards.gist: Umbrella name for any milk or cream set by egg over gentle heat
cards.guest: It's milk or cream gently cooked with eggs until it thickens into something smooth and silky. It can be a spoonable pudding, a pie filling or a sauce.
cards.why: Egg proteins unwind and link as they warm, trapping the liquid into a soft gel. Stirred on the stove it stays pourable. Baked in a water bath it sets firm enough to slice or unmold. Too much heat and the eggs tighten and weep, so it is cooked low and slow.
cards.note: A baked custard should still jiggle slightly in the center. Bubbles, holes or weeping mean it was overcooked.
cards.pairs: Fresh berries, caramel, nutmeg, pie crust, stewed fruit
cards.line: Buttermilk custard pie, macerated strawberries

cards.gist: Chopped chocolate melted into hot cream, glossy and smooth
cards.guest: It's chocolate melted into warm cream until it's glossy and smooth. It's the silky center of a truffle and the shiny glaze on a chocolate cake.
cards.why: Hot cream poured over chopped chocolate melts it, and stirring emulsifies the cocoa butter and cream into one smooth mass. The ratio sets the texture: equal parts pours as a glaze or whips into frosting, twice as much chocolate sets firm enough to roll.
cards.pairs: Tart fillings, cake glaze, macaron filling, sea salt, raspberry
cards.notThis: Not a truffle itself. This is the mixture, and a truffle is a ball rolled from it.
cards.line: Dark chocolate ganache tart, sea salt, crème fraîche

cards.gist: Chilled sweet dish made airy with whipped cream or beaten egg whites
cards.guest: It's a chilled dessert, often chocolate, lightened with whipped cream or egg whites. Rich flavor, but it melts away and never sits heavy.
cards.why: A flavored base, often melted chocolate or fruit puree, has whipped cream or beaten egg whites folded through it, then chills until the fat or a little gelatin holds the bubbles in place. The trapped air is what makes it taste rich but eat light.
cards.note: Classic chocolate versions are often made with uncooked eggs. Ask the kitchen how theirs is made.
cards.notThis: Not a soufflé, which is baked and served hot. Not pot de crème, which is baked dense in a cup.
cards.line: Dark chocolate mousse, olive oil, sea salt

cards.gist: Sliced frozen mold of whipped yolks and cream, or layers in a tall glass
cards.guest: In France it's a frozen dessert of whipped yolks and cream, sliced from a mold, softer and silkier than ice cream. At brunch it's layered yogurt and fruit.
cards.why: The French version cooks yolks with hot sugar syrup, whips them pale and thick, folds in whipped cream and freezes it in a mold. All that air keeps it soft enough to slice. In America the word means layers of ice cream or yogurt with fruit in a tall glass.
cards.origin: French for perfect, the frozen dessert of French pastry
cards.notThis: On a starter menu, chicken liver parfait is a silky savory pâté, not a dessert.
cards.line: Frozen nougat parfait, raspberry coulis, almond tuile

cards.gist: Sweet cream set with gelatin, turned out soft and wobbly
cards.guest: It's sweet cream, gently set so it just holds its shape and trembles on the plate. Cool, silky and clean, usually with fruit alongside.
cards.why: Cream and sugar are warmed with vanilla, gelatin is stirred in, and it sets in the fridge in a mold, then is turned out. The gelatin gives a soft wobble rather than the denser body of an egg custard, so it tastes of pure, clean dairy.
cards.origin: Italian for cooked cream, from Piedmont in the north
cards.pairs: Berries, stone fruit, caramel, aged balsamic, honey
cards.line: Vanilla bean panna cotta, macerated strawberries

cards.gist: Bite-size ball of cocoa and cream, rolled in cocoa powder or dipped
cards.guest: It's a little ball of chocolate and cream, soft and rich, that melts on the tongue. A one-bite way to end a meal.
cards.why: A firm, chocolate-heavy ganache is chilled, scooped and rolled into balls, then dusted in cocoa, rolled in nuts or dipped in a hard chocolate shell. The cream keeps the center soft, so it melts on the tongue far faster than a solid bar.
cards.note: Best at cool room temperature. Straight from the fridge the center is hard and the flavor muted.
cards.origin: French sweet named for its look-alike, the dusty black truffle fungus
cards.notThis: Not the truffle mushroom. If a guest asks about truffle on a dessert menu, it is this sweet.
cards.line: House chocolate truffles, cocoa dusted

cards.gist: Italian frozen dessert, more milk and less air, served softer and warmer
cards.guest: It's Italian ice cream, denser and silkier, served a little softer so the flavor comes through bright and strong.
cards.why: The base leans on milk more than cream, so it is lower in fat. It is churned slowly, beating in less air, which makes it dense. It is served a few degrees warmer than ice cream, so it is soft and less numbing, and the flavor hits harder.
cards.origin: Italian for frozen, from the verb gelare, to freeze
cards.notThis: Not ice cream with an accent. Ice cream has more cream and air and is served colder and firmer.
cards.line: Pistachio gelato, olive oil, flaky salt

cards.gist: Sweet juice or coffee frozen into loose, grainy ice crystals
cards.guest: It's a Sicilian ice of sweet fruit, coffee or almond, frozen into fine, icy crystals. Light and refreshing.
cards.why: The flavored syrup is stirred slowly as it freezes, in a machine in Sicilian bars or with a fork in a pan, so it sets as ice crystals rather than a smooth, airy mass. It melts fast and tastes clean, like a grown-up snow cone with the flavor frozen in.
cards.origin: Sicily, from Italian grana, grain, for its grainy crystals
cards.pairs: Brioche for dipping, whipped cream, espresso
cards.notThis: Not sorbet, which is churned smooth and scoops. Granita is spooned as loose, grainy crystals.
cards.line: Espresso granita, whipped cream, candied orange

cards.gist: Fruit-sugar frozen dessert churned with a small splash of milk
cards.guest: It's a fruit ice with milk or cream churned in. Brighter than ice cream, creamier than sorbet.
cards.why: It is a sorbet base of fruit and sugar with a small amount of dairy added, about 1 to 2 percent milkfat in the US. That bit of milk fat softens the ice crystals and rounds the tartness, so it sits between a clean sorbet and a rich ice cream.
cards.origin: From Turkish and Persian sherbet, a chilled sweet fruit drink
cards.notThis: Not sorbet, whose classic base is fruit and sugar. Often said sherbert, but there is only one r in the word.
cards.line: Orange sherbet, shortbread, mint

cards.gist: Smooth churned fruit ice on sugar syrup, clean and sharp
cards.guest: It's a fruit ice churned smooth like ice cream. Pure, bright fruit flavor that feels light after a big meal.
cards.why: Fruit puree or juice is balanced with sugar syrup and churned while it freezes. The sugar keeps the crystals tiny, so it scoops smooth like ice cream, but as a base built on fruit and sugar it tastes sharper and cleaner and it melts quickly.
cards.note: A small scoop between courses is a palate cleanser. Most sorbets melt faster than ice cream, so run them straight out.
cards.notThis: Not sherbet, which has some milk churned in, and not granita, which is grainy rather than smooth.
cards.line: Blood orange sorbet, pistachio, mint

cards.gist: Rich, high-fat dairy base churned with plenty of air to scoop
cards.guest: It's cream, milk and sugar, often with egg yolk, churned as it freezes until thick and smooth. Rich and soft enough to scoop.
cards.why: Cream, milk and sugar, often cooked with egg yolks into a custard, are churned as they freeze. Churning keeps ice crystals tiny and beats in air, so it scoops soft. It holds more fat and air than gelato, so it tastes richer but a little less dense.
cards.pairs: Warm pie, brownies, affogato, fruit crisp
cards.notThis: Not gelato, which is churned slower with more milk and less cream, so it is denser and softer.
cards.line: Vanilla bean ice cream, warm apple crisp

cards.gist: Italian frozen mousse, soft enough to slice when frozen
cards.guest: It's an Italian frozen mousse, whipped eggs and cream frozen in a mold and sliced. Soft and airy, it melts on your tongue.
cards.why: Egg yolks and sugar are whisked over heat into a foam, then folded with whipped cream and frozen without churning. All that air keeps it soft enough to slice straight from the freezer, lighter and more like a frozen mousse than ice cream.
cards.note: Some versions fold in whipped egg white that is never cooked. Ask the kitchen how theirs is made.
cards.origin: Italian for half cold, for its soft, never rock-hard set
cards.notThis: Close cousin of the French frozen parfait. A layered glass parfait of yogurt and fruit is another thing.
cards.line: Honey semifreddo, roasted figs, pistachio

cards.gist: Chilled baked custard under a thin crust of torched sugar
cards.guest: It's a cold vanilla custard with a layer of sugar torched to glassy caramel. You crack the top with your spoon.
cards.why: Cream, egg yolks, sugar and vanilla bake gently in a water bath until just set, then chill. Sugar is burned on top to order, so you get a warm, brittle caramel shell over cold, silky custard. The contrast is the whole point.
cards.origin: French, meaning burnt cream
cards.line: Vanilla bean crème brûlée, fresh berries

cards.gist: Soft-set, silky baked custard in its own little cup, often chocolate
cards.guest: It's a rich baked custard served in a little cup, usually deep chocolate. Silky and spoonable, like the best pudding.
cards.why: Cream, milk and egg yolks, often with melted chocolate, bake gently in small cups in a water bath. It uses more yolk and less white than a firm custard, so it sets soft and dense, eaten with a spoon from the cup and never turned out.
cards.origin: French, pot of cream, named for the small lidded cups it bakes in
cards.notThis: Not mousse, which is whipped and airy. Not crème brûlée, which has a torched sugar top.
cards.line: Dark chocolate pot de crème, sea salt, whipped cream

cards.gist: Thick stovetop custard set with starch, piped into eclairs
cards.guest: It's a thick vanilla custard, the filling inside eclairs and under the fruit on a tart. Smooth, rich and not too sweet.
cards.why: Milk, egg yolks and sugar are cooked on the stove with flour or cornstarch and brought to a boil. The starch lets it thicken until it holds its shape when piped or sliced, where a crème anglaise, thickened by yolks alone, stays pourable.
cards.pairs: Eclairs, fruit tarts, Boston cream pie, cream puffs
cards.notThis: Not crème anglaise, the pourable sauce thickened by yolks alone. This is thick enough to pipe.
cards.line: Fresh berry tart, vanilla pastry cream

cards.gist: Cream whipped soft with sugar and vanilla to spoonable peaks
cards.guest: It is fresh cream whipped with a little sugar and vanilla, soft and cloud-light. The classic spoonful on berries, shortcake or a slice of pie.
cards.why: Cold cream is whisked until its fat droplets trap air, roughly doubling in volume, with sugar and vanilla added near the end. Stopped at soft peaks it stays silky and melts on the tongue. Whipped too far it turns grainy and heads toward butter.
cards.origin: French, named for the Chantilly estate north of Paris
cards.pairs: Fresh berries, strawberry shortcake, meringue, choux
cards.notThis: Not pastry cream, the thick cooked custard. This is raw cream lifted by whipped-in air.
cards.line: Strawberry shortcake, Chantilly cream, mint
